This paper delves into online Reinforcement Learning (RL) within partially observable dynamic systems, particularly focusing on Predictive State Representations (PSRs). The PSRs model captures prominent models like POMDP and describes states through a set of future observation predictions, solely reliant on observable quantities. A new algorithm for PSRs is introduced, capable of learning nearly optimal policies at a sample complexity scaling in line with system parameters, without being bound by large state and observation spaces. Our algorithm seamlessly integrates function approximation for complex systems. Notably, given a suitable model class, the algorithm showcases sample complexity growth that scales polynomially with model complexity, rather than the size of the state and observation spaces. Our findings mark the first time a polynomial sample complexity is achieved to match the globally optimal policy in PSRs. Lastly, a general theorem derived here can be directly applied to establish sample complexity bounds for specific models like POMDP variants, POMDPs with low-rank transitions and linear emission.

Significant reductions in the costs associated with neural network inference may be achieved through efficient matrix multiplication approximations. Building upon previous research that employed fast hash functions to substitute costly multiplications with table lookups from training data, this work offers improvements tailored to the deep learning inference context, where training data and pre-learned model weight matrices are accessible. Additionally, this work presents a fine-tuning procedure to accelerate neural networks without compromising accuracy. We evaluate our proposed approach on an image classification task and observe improvements over prior methods but note a considerable decrease in classification accuracy when compared to exact matrix multiplication. Although this work presents a less than ideal outcome, it provides a direction for future research on accelerating inner product computations using rapid nonlinear hashing methods.

We carry out detailed calculations of Vafa-Witten invariants of 3-dimensional manifolds, building on similar Floer group computations in Donaldson theory. We perform explicit calculations of these invariants for specific instances involving various surgical operations like the Gluck twist, knot surgeries, and log-transforms, providing insights into the invariants' general properties. We outline anticipated properties for arbitrary 3-manifolds, encompassing the behavior of modular groups, connections to Floer homology, the infinite-dimensional nature of these invariants, and the absence of instanton effects.

In models that extend the Standard Model by additional Higgs particles, such as the Two-Higgs-Doublet-Model, heavy doublet-dominant Higgs bosons are potential targets for study at high-energy colliders, including the Large Hadron Collider. However, these bosons are subject to strict decay constraints imposed by the SU(2)_{L} symmetry for sufficiently heavy states. When considering only extra Higgs doublets, fermionic decays typically become dominant, but certain bosonic modes can offer clearer signals. Conversely, models that incorporate singlet states along with doublet-dominant Higgs particles can exhibit drastically different behavior, including enhanced bosonic decay channels, provided the singlet-dominant scalars are accessible kinematically. To interpret the experimental data meaningfully, a comprehensive understanding of the model, including radiative corrections, is necessary. This paper specifically investigates the full one-loop-order bosonic decays of heavy doublet-dominant Higgs particles within the MSSM and NMSSM frameworks, emphasizing the SU(2)_{L} symmetry and its consequences, such as significant non-resonant contributions to final states consisting of three bosons.

Our research reveals that discontinuous shear thickening can occur within both dilute and moderately packed inertial suspensions comprising smooth particles. DST can be viewed as a phase transition triggered in inertial suspensions, where the system transitions abruptly between states. A related kinetic model accurately aligns with findings from numerical Langevin simulations across a broad spectrum of the mixture's concentration, achieved without relying on any adjustable parameters.

A key component of achieving sustainable development and climate objectives is the effective management of dam reservoirs. Unfortunately, small-scale dam reservoirs are often overlooked due to limited information about their geographical location. To bridge this data gap, utilizing high-resolution remote sensing imagery offers a promising approach, specifically a subcategory of water body extraction known as dam reservoir identification. This process involves isolating water features in images, followed by distinguishing dam reservoirs from natural waterbodies. To achieve this, our proposed methodology utilizes a novel, two-part deep learning framework. Initially, it uses a segmentation model to separate waterbodies from background landscapes, with a secondary classification model to determine whether each identified water body is a dam reservoir or natural body. In order to address complexities surrounding water-land boundaries, our framework incorporates a technique that involves learning through point-level comparisons across images. In a separate step, our framework employs an additional metric learning approach that focuses on clusters, refining image embedding through fine-grained optimization. To support ongoing research, a comprehensive dataset has been created using earth imagery data along with manually annotated reservoirs in West African and Indian river basins. Thorough evaluations on this dataset reveal the superior effectiveness of our proposed method when compared to state-of-the-art approaches in tasks involving water body segmentation, dam reservoir identification and combined dam reservoir extraction.

In microelectronic devices, local stress and strain fluctuations at microscopic scales can impair functionality, make components more susceptible to thermal and radiation damage, and limit device reliability. Characterizing these fluctuations using conventional methods is impractical due to their tiny scale. This study successfully applies non-destructive differential aperture X-ray microscopy to detect stress and strain concentrations within microelectronic devices, specifically in the depth-resolved analysis of a gallium nitride layer in high electron mobility transistors. The technique provides high-resolution two-dimensional strain maps, showing how the strain distribution changes after exposure to gamma radiation, resulting in significant lattice plane contraction attributed to radiation-induced damage in the device components bonded to the gallium nitride layer.

Determining how well software-based medical devices with AI functionality perform under real-world variations is vital for assessing their effectiveness and reliability before use in hospitals. Due to strict regulations surrounding medical device software and the scarcity of extensive labeled medical datasets, we explore a method to predict the accuracy of any given AI model on a previously unseen patient population without modifying its initial training process or making assumptions about its original training data. We present a novel method using conformal prediction, which doesn't require access to internal model workings or the source data it was trained on. We test this approach alongside other techniques using data from medical imaging fields such as breast imaging, skin condition analysis, and tissue examination under various scenarios of real-world data variation. Our goal is to help device manufacturers develop and employ standardized testing protocols for AI tools, thereby increasing their dependability and reliability in clinical settings.

We have developed a novel forward modeling technique for predicting galaxy redshift distributions using photometric surveys. The framework consists of multiple components: a comprehensive model of galaxy populations, which accounts for the physical characteristics of galaxies and galaxy evolution; a synthesis model linking the physical properties of galaxies to their observable photometric properties; a characterization model detailing the observation and calibration processes for specific surveys; and explicit handling of selection criteria to ensure accurate results. This forward modeling approach has distinct advantages, including its reliance on photometric data alone and explicit control over modeling assumptions, enabling a direct link between photometric redshift inference and galaxy evolution physics. In addition to estimating redshift distributions, forward modeling can also provide robust inferences about the broader statistical properties of galaxy populations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the Galaxy And Mass Assembly and Vimos VLT Deep surveys and comparing our predictions to their spectroscopic redshifts. The results show that our baseline model accurately predicts tomographic redshift distributions for these surveys with a high degree of accuracy, meeting the requirements of Stage III cosmological surveys. We anticipate that further refinements and hyper-parameter fitting will enable forward modeling to provide accurate redshift distribution inference for even more demanding Stage IV surveys.

A biped walking model, grounded on a solvable inverted pendulum concept with 
two massless, articulated legs capable of stable locomotion on sloping surfaces 
and uneven terrain, has been developed. The biped's gait arises from the interplay 
between the pendular motion of a stationary leg and the articulated movement of 
the trailing leg, facilitated by the sequential switching of the legs' roles 
and the conservation of the pendular motion's energy. Stable locomotion on 
uneven surfaces and sloping planes is achievable through consistent leg angles 
and stride time adjustments. This closed-form solvable model accurately represents 
bipedal motion types, and optimization results for stride speed are correlated 
with the robot's parameters.

Our investigation into how insoluble surfactants influence turbulent jets focuses on their spatio-temporal development. Through the use of three-dimensional numerical simulations, which take into account surfactant-driven Marangoni stresses using an interface-tracking/level-set method, this study further builds upon our prior research. That previous study, which appeared in 2021 in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics, examined the intricate interaction between vortices and surfaces in the absence of surfactants. Here, numerical results are generated for various ranges of Weber and elasticity numbers where surface deformation and Marangoni stresses generated from surfactant concentration gradients contribute to vorticity production. Notably, this study reveals for the first time that Marangoni stresses have a significant impact on the formation of long-lived, hairpin-like vortex structures. The emergence of these coherent structures plays a crucial role in determining the three-dimensional behavior of the interface. Theoretical equations describing the mechanisms driving the production of circulation in surfactant-containing, three-dimensional two-phase flows are also presented. Notably, these equations highlight the major contribution made by Marangoni stresses to this process.

To understand how radiation impacts the formation of globular clusters, a series of computational simulations mimicked a massive collision of turbulent molecular clouds. By modeling scenarios with and without stellar radiation, the study found that a gravitationally bound star cluster forms within 3 million years. However, this cluster doesn't develop from a single collapse but rather through the merger of local dense gas clumps and gas accumulation. In these simulations, radiation absorption played a key role in suppressing gas collapse, and efficient photoionization occurs once enough stars have formed. Without radiation feedback, the simulated cluster mass increased by nearly 2 times. Accounting for intense Lyman-alpha radiation had a slightly more pronounced effect, increasing the mass difference by 16 percent. In scenarios incorporating radiation, supernovae occur after star-forming clouds disperse, and their metal-enriched material isn't immediately reused for star formation.

Supposons que $X$ soit une variété projective lisse définie sur un corps de nombres, avec $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0$. Ensuite, Colliot-Thélène et Raskind ont montré que le groupe de torsion $CH^2(X)_{tors}$ dans le groupe de Chow de cycles de codimension 2 est fini. Dans cette note, nous établissons des limites uniformes pour ce groupe fini lorsqu'il varie au sein d'une famille de variétés $X$. 

(Suppose $X$ be a smooth projective variety defined over a number field, with $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0$. Then, Colliot-Thélène and Raskind showed that the torsion group $CH^2(X)_{tors}$ in the Chow group of cycles of codimension 2 is finite. In this note, we establish uniform limits for this finite group when it varies within a family of varieties $X$.

In superconducting quantum devices such as qubits and sensors, excess quasiparticles are key components to understand. We investigate the behavior of these quasiparticles in finite-length weak links, which have several subgap states that can be measured by a microwave resonator, allowing the detection of even/odd parity. According to our model, precise control over parity can be achieved by applying a tailored microwave pulse, which induces polarization in one parity state by targeting a specific transition in the opposing state. This theoretical framework explains recent observations and offers practical advice for optimizing parity control in Josephson junctions made of semiconducting nanowires, providing valuable insights for the manipulation of Andreev qubits.

This study broadens existing findings on generalized solitons known as $q$-solitons by examining the full scenario involving non-compact solitons. By setting standards for the regularity of vector field $X$ and curvature conditions on manifold $M$, we utilize the chosen characteristics of tensor $q$ to establish that such non-compact $q$-solitons are stationary and $q$-flat. We conclude with a practical application of our findings to ambient obstruction solitons, Cotton solitons, and Bach solitons, highlighting the versatility of these general theorems across different types of flows.

The initial stages of binary star systems with exoplanets are influenced by star-forming clusters which can lead to the dynamic evolution of these binary-planet systems. Numerical simulations were conducted to model the interactions between planets similar to the solar system's four gas giants and a binary companion of half a solar mass, both within a cluster environment. The results showed that nearly 10% of these systems become unstable due to perturbations from the cluster environment pushing the binary orbit towards the planets. This destabilization occurs even when systems initially have stable configurations, resulting in the removal of smaller planets and the increased eccentricity of surviving larger ones. Many systems that destabilize will also lose their binary companions before the cluster disperses, making them appear as hosts of eccentric exoplanets formed in isolation. The simulated cluster-driven evolution can also create planetary systems with mismatched spin-orbit angles by making the system precess as a single unit under the influence of an inclined binary, with systems having the largest spin-orbit angles typically retaining their binary companion and maintaining multiple planets.

Neural networks are able to approximate non-linear functions that are often complex, which can be expressed through a series of mathematical operations or treated as a black box system. A fundamental type of neural network known as DeepONet, which is based on a theory of approximation, was introduced in 2019 and has been followed by several more general neural operators based on graph neural networks and Fourier transforms. While neural operators rely primarily on data for training when the underlying systems are unknown, it is possible to incorporate governing equations into the learning process when these systems are well understood, resulting in physics-informed neural operators. By acting as surrogates, these networks have numerous applications in real-time inference, uncertainty quantification, autonomous systems, and design optimization. Moreover, independently trained DeepONets can be used to model complex multi-physics systems with relatively low computational requirements. This work provides a comprehensive overview of DeepONet, the Fourier neural operator, the graph neural operator, as well as their extensions and adaptations, which have the potential to transform a variety of applications in computational mechanics, including fluid mechanics, porous media, and solid mechanics.

Predicting emotions is a vital aspect of mental health and emotion-driven technology, yet its intricacy stemming from the interplay between an individual's physical well-being, mental status, and external surroundings makes it an extremely difficult task. Our research utilizes mobile sensor data to forecast happiness and stress, taking into account both the user's physiological attributes and environmental factors like weather and social interactions. Leveraging phone data to build social graphs, we develop an innovative machine learning framework that combines insights from various users within a network while integrating the temporal aspects of the data to accurately predict emotions for all participants. The construction of these social graphs does not incur extra expenses or compromise user data privacy. Our suggested architecture automates social network integration for affect prediction, effectively handling dynamic social networks and scaling seamlessly to large-scale networks. The thorough evaluation we conducted demonstrates the enhancement achieved through incorporating social networks, while also examining how the network topology affects the model's performance.

Complex liquid formations in fluids are characterized by unsteady interfaces, often observed during splashing or atomization, which lead to intricate geometries. To capture the essence of these geometries efficiently, we apply skeletonization to minimize the information needed for their description. In our investigation, a modified technique for skeletonizing multiphase flows with a sharp interface is employed, which involves diffusing an index function while simultaneously moving the interfaces, resulting in the formation of skeleton structures. These skeletons retain the fundamental topological features of the fluid jets, along with a record of the interface movement and volume accumulation during the process. We examine various quantitative metrics, including branch length distribution and the Topology Morphology Descriptor, to quantify and distinguish the skeletons, effectively providing a condensed representation of their topology.

The intricacies of Recommender Systems (RSs) largely stem from their use in multifaceted applications and impact user experience through diverse user interfaces. 

Research to date has primarily concentrated on RSs' ability to generate precise item rankings, overlooking the evaluation of RS behavior in realistic contexts. 

This narrow focus restricts the potential for RSs to make lasting, real-world impressions and renders them susceptible to detrimental behavior, such as amplifying data prejudices. 

To encourage collaboration among practitioners and cultivate novel methodologies for testing RSs in authentic environments, we introduce EvalRS, a novel type of challenge.

Understanding human-object interactions in a visual scene is crucial and requires recognizing spatial connections between humans and objects to accurately infer interactions. Our proposed approach, SGCN4HOI, employs a graph-based technique to model human-object interactions by incorporating human and object keypoints through a graph convolutional network. SGCN4HOI combines spatial, visual, and geometric features from human-object pairs and utilizes a novel representation of object keypoints based on their structural information. Our model outperforms existing pose-based methods in benchmark evaluations, such as the V-COCO dataset, and demonstrates competitive results against other detection models.

In Europe, delays in the expansion of electricity transmission have been prevalent in recent years, hindering the integration of renewable energy. Developing a hydrogen network utilizing existing fossil gas infrastructure could meet demand for low-emission fuels, mitigate the impact of variable renewable energy sources, and prevent costly power grid expansions. Our research explores the feasibility of this approach by adjusting the expansion of electricity and hydrogen grids within a low-carbon European energy system characterized by high levels of renewable energy production. Our simulations span 181 regions and all sectors, including electricity, buildings, transport, agriculture, and industry, at a high spatiotemporal resolution. The findings demonstrate the value of a hydrogen network connecting high-productivity areas with consumption centers, synthetic fuel production sites, and geologically-stored hydrogen sites. Establishing such a network can decrease overall system costs by as much as 6%, with the greatest benefits realized when power grid enhancements are impossible. Furthermore, approximately 58-66% of the hydrogen network can be constructed using repurposed natural gas pipelines. Nevertheless, the results also indicate that hydrogen networks and grid expansions are not mutually exclusive, as combining the two can achieve the greatest cost savings of 12%.

We use data from the Dark Energy Survey's first three years, in conjunction with external data, to refine the $\Lambda$CDM model. Our analysis involves the correlation functions of weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we employ simulated data and blinded real-data analyses. Our study covers five extensions to the $\Lambda$CDM model: dark energy with time-varying equation of state, non-zero spatial curvature, sterile neutrinos, modified gravity, and a model probing the growth of structure via binned $\sigma_8(z)$ measurements. Our analysis reveals that for dark energy with time-varying equation of state, evaluated at the pivot redshift, the best fit parameters are $(-0.99^{+0.28}_{-0.17}, -0.9\pm 1.2)$ at 68% confidence with $z_{\rm p}=0.24$, based on DES measurements alone, and $(-1.03^{+0.04}_{-0.03}, -0.4^{+0.4}_{-0.3})$ with $z_{\rm p}=0.21$, when combining all data. Spatial curvature constraints from external data give us $\Omega_k=0.0009\pm 0.0017$ and $N_{\rm eff}=3.10^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$. The study also places tighter bounds on the mass of sterile neutrinos, improving the previous limits by a factor of three. Furthermore, our research puts limits on modifications to the lensing and Poisson equations. Our overall findings suggest no significant evidence for physics beyond $\Lambda$CDM.

Schmidt's latest research involves finding commonalities among generalized bent functions, cocyclic Butson Hadamard matrices, and abelian splitting relative difference sets. This research expands on previous findings by exploring broader equivalences in Butson matrices that share a shared cyclic pattern rather than strict group invariance. This development has significant practical uses, including designing Boolean functions that incorporate partially bent characteristics even in cases where a traditional bent function is impossible to create.

Short-pulsed electron beams of durations between femtoseconds to picoseconds provide unparalleled avenues to investigate dynamic areas such as molecular motion and radiation effects at extremely high doses. This research introduces a simple method to produce electron beams of MeV magnitude in ambient air by tightly focusing an ultra-high intensity femtosecond infrared laser beam. A dose rate of 0.15 Gy/s achieved one meter away from the source would surpass the annual safe exposure limit in just one second, underscoring the necessity for implementing safety measures. Computer simulations validating that the acceleration of particles is driven by the relativistic ponderomotive force confirm the results and reveal that this approach's potential for growth aligns with the advancement of higher power lasers, also offering a potential method for Flash radiation therapy.

Quantum speed limits set the minimum duration for physical processes by establishing the maximum rate at which quantum systems can change their state or be measured. We extend this concept to describe the evolution of quantum systems through unitary operator transformations, which have far-reaching implications across both quantum and classical systems. We identify and analyze two different speed limits, and investigate how these speed limits may interact, using a qubit and a random matrix as examples. Our work has significant implications for the study of quantum systems out of equilibrium, and provides valuable constraints for the prediction of quantum response and estimation precision.

This paper introduces a three-dimensional reconfigurable robot comprising cubes, actuated by electromagnets that facilitate 3D reconfiguration through pivoting. Although multiple actuation methods for self-reconfigurable robots have been studied, they frequently face issues of high production costs, complexity, assembly needs, and size requirements, limiting mass production. To resolve this issue, our approach uses electromagnets embedded within the cube's edges to create complementary and opposing magnetic fields. By leveraging attractive forces for hinge formation and repulsive forces for pivoting maneuvers, our robot can be rearranged by voxelizing it into constituent modules known as Electrovoxels, and then reconfiguring them through electromagnetic actuation. To demonstrate its capabilities, we developed untethered, three-dimensional self-reconfigurable robots and successfully tested their 2D and 3D reconfiguration using various movements on an air-table and during microgravity conditions. This paper outlines the hardware design of our robot, its pivoting framework, our reconfiguration software, and an evaluation of the dynamic and electrical characteristics of our system to facilitate the development of large-scale self-reconfigurable robots.

This research focuses on noisy matrix completion, the process of reconstructing a low-rank matrix from incomplete and inaccurate data. By establishing uniform sampling and incoherence assumptions, it's demonstrated that a noise-independent, square-root-based matrix completion algorithm achieves optimal performance in solving noisy matrix completion problems. Similar to its high-dimensional linear regression counterpart, the square-root-based algorithm's noise-agnostic nature is key to its success. Although it results in a convex program, the algorithm's statistical performance is linked to its inherent connections with a non-convex rank-constrained model.

This article explores a simplified version of Calderon's problem, specifically focusing on high-order polyharmonic operators, to establish a key finding inspired by Calderon's initial work, where the determination of certain coefficients is uniquely defined through an inversion process of a related transform, ultimately providing insight into a key aspect of this problem.

Protoplanetary disks with irregular shapes create an ideal environment for pressure traps to form. One significant hurdle in planetary formation is the meter-sized threshold, which significantly restricts the growth pace of planets. Researchers have proposed various solutions to this barrier, including pressure traps - localized areas where disk pressure deviates from the general pattern, causing planetesimal drift to stop. Despite ongoing research, the origins of pressure traps remain unclear, including their specific configurations. Deformed disks are common among accretion disks in general, including protoplanetary disks. We propose that such irregular disks are key to forming pressure traps, which facilitate breaking through the meter-sized barrier. By analyzing pressure traps formed through external torque, we explore their implications for early planetary formation across different settings like circumbinary disks and gap edges.

A novel approach to analyzing generalized parton distributions, based on conformal moment expansion, is proposed for a comprehensive understanding. The framework utilizes a universal moment parameterization strategy to simultaneously accommodate collinear parton distribution functions derived from phenomenology and generalized form factors obtained from lattice calculations. The versatility of the parameterization also enables fitting of direct lattice calculations for generalized parton distributions. The current work focuses on analyzing t-dependent parton distribution functions, a limiting case of generalized parton distributions. The approach, applicable to both the xi not equals 0 and xi not equals 0 regions with the inclusion of extra parameters, allows for future experimental observable fitting. The utility of the framework is demonstrated through an example fitting of generalized parton distributions, illustrating the quark transverse angular momentum densities and the quark impact parameter space distributions within both unpolarized and transversely polarized protons.

A new framework for analyzing directed acyclic graphs is presented by leveraging
categorical probability theory. In this approach, we introduce a concept of causal
models and a corresponding notion of d-separation, allowing for a more abstract
evaluation of compatibility. This framework offers several advantages, including a
more intuitive criterion that utilizes topological connections. Furthermore, its
results extend beyond probability theory, applying to deterministic and
possibilistic networks, thereby providing a comprehensive proof of the
equivalence between local and global Markov properties and causal
compatibility for a wide range of variables, including both continuous and
deterministic types.

Research into twisted two-dimensional material layers has become increasingly vital for understanding quantum states, with their moir\'e patterns leading to unique electronic behavior. Despite the prevalence of 2D materials, the study of these structures remains relatively underdeveloped. This study develops a comprehensive mathematical framework for analyzing the properties of moir\'e patterns in twisted Janus transition metal dichalcogenides, accounting for structural changes and interactions between layers. By exploring numerous potential combinations of materials and layer arrangements, the model reveals that emergent electronic behavior is highly dependent on material composition, layer orientation, and twist angle. The study opens up new possibilities for understanding the complex electronic properties of these structures and discovering novel phenomena that can be harnessed and controlled.

We examine the initial distortion of space-time by observing dark matter structure. Considering the possibility of an unusual pattern in the distortion at small scales, we use a semi-theoretical approach to track how large and small clumps of matter in this distortion change over time, while accounting for possible errors in estimating the effect of external forces on the growth of smaller clumps. This allows us to establish a new, more robust limit on the distortion at small scales based on the number of dwarf galaxies observed in our galaxy and observations of stellar streams. This limit sets the maximum size of an unusual distortion at about one in 10 million million for patterns at about one thousand times the distance between stars. Furthermore, we find that an unusual distortion like this one, if present, could boost signals for indirect detection of dark matter by up to a factor of 10,000 within the current range of acceptable distortions.

A retinal feature that captures a specific aspect of an image can be condensed into a single numerical value for further statistical analysis. Nevertheless, extracting a single, meaningful value from a complex image is a challenging task, typically necessitating multi-step pipelines that require high-quality images. Consequently, researchers often have to exclude a considerable portion of available data due to image quality issues. To mitigate this, we propose an innovative method called Deep Approximation of Retinal Traits (DART), where a neural network can replicate the output of existing high-quality image analysis pipelines on synthetically degraded images. In our research, DART effectively replicates the output of VAMPIRE, an existing method for calculating the Fractal Dimension (FD) in retinal images from the UK Biobank. The results show excellent agreement between our method and VAMPIRE, even with severely degraded images. This suggests the potential to significantly reduce data exclusion rates. Additionally, DART can process images at an impressive rate of over 1,000 per second using a single GPU. The positive outcomes of our research encourage further development of DART as a useful tool for retinal analysis.

The explosive merger of two neutron stars creates high-velocity ejected matter, reaching velocities that are 60% of the speed of light and faster. A study into this phenomenon reveals the production of radio to X-ray radiation through shock waves formed by these fast ejecta as they interact with the surrounding space. Analytic models are developed to simulate this interaction for spherical ejections of matter, with varying power distributions based on the energy levels and velocities. For scenarios typical of these neutron star mergers, a proposed model with both gentle and steep power distribution segments offers a precise prediction of the emitted radiation flux, even when the ejecta decelerate. This improvement over earlier predictions, based on extreme energy scenarios, enables more accurate inferences about ejected matter from observational data. For instance, a similar merger event such as GW170817 is expected to produce detectable radiation over a time span of about 10,000 days.

Laboratory-grown icicles formed from slightly contaminated water exhibit distinctive ripples, whose near-universal wavelength suggests a morphological origin. We conducted experiments using artificial impurities and observed that a portion of the contaminants became embedded within the ice, giving rise to internal inclusions. These inclusions were found to arrange in a specific pattern aligned with the ripple peaks, consisting of chevron structures that themselves comprise crescent-shaped components. We also studied the crystal structure of artificially created icicles with and without contaminants, and provide an in-depth analysis of the growth patterns found within icicles.

The importance of spontaneous conversations for our well-being and developing effective social interaction is undeniable. Previous research focused on conversation quality has typically viewed it through a narrow lens, prioritizing in-depth discussions over casual small talk. Conversely, studies examining interaction experiences have indirectly measured conversation quality through related constructs like rapport and engagement. In this work, we aim to fill the knowledge gap by introducing a comprehensive approach to defining conversation quality. Based on the collaborative aspects of cooperative communication, we've developed and validated two assessment tools that gauge conversation quality from individual and group perspectives. We propose capturing raters' holistic impressions of conversation participants' experiences from observing their behavior and validate these findings using the MatchNMingle dataset, featuring real-life conversations. Additionally, our analysis of behavioral traits that correlate with high-quality conversations reveals that raters associate higher conversation quality with smaller groups, equitable turn-taking with minimal interruptions, and synchronized bodily movement with shorter response times.

This study presents BRILLsson, a groundbreaking binary neural network architecture for speech tasks that don't rely on semantics.
BRILLsson is trained with knowledge transfer from a comprehensive, real-valued TRILLsson model, requiring a tiny fraction of its training dataset.
As a result, the compact BRILLsson models measure just 2MB in size and operate within an 8ms latency threshold, making them ideal for resource-constrained devices, such as wearable technology.
BRILLsson is assessed across eight evaluation tasks, including spoken language recognition, sentiment analysis, disease diagnosis, and audio event detection, and consistently demonstrates parity in performance with larger, more complex models.

Researchers studying fairness in machine learning have converged on key definitions for fair models, known as fairness criteria, but they have inherent drawbacks. To overcome these limitations, we pinpoint four significant shortcomings in existing criteria, and propose enhancing performative prediction through a distributionally robust objective.

We consider the possibility that primordial black holes, formed during the universe's early stages, retain an electric charge down to the present day. Our findings suggest that PBHs would have acquired a non-zero charge at the time of their formation due to random variations and particle collisions. Although these initial charges could have been neutralized by rapid discharge processes, we discover that magnetic fields generated by rotating black holes can divert them, preventing loss to infinity, regardless of PBH mass. Additionally, we find that rotating charged PBHs can produce magnetic fields strong enough to counteract the effects of charge dissipation for masses over 1 kilogram, and also neutralize Hawking radiation for larger masses. This could allow charged PBHs to maintain their charge for a longer period. In the later universe, we conclude that PBHs residing in dark matter halos could accumulate an overall average negative charge. Calculations show that PBHs with masses approximately 10^20 kg and 10^30 kg could possess charges in the order of -10^-32 C/kg and -10^-22 C/kg, respectively. Given that this charge falls below the limit required for discharge, we find that PBHs could potentially remain non-neutral to this day. Combining initial charge, charge protection, and late-time negative charge accumulation, our research indicates that PBHs of all masses may carry a net charge, roughly two to ten orders of magnitude lower than the limit imposed by sub-extreme Reissner-Nordstrom black holes, and even comparable to the extremal charge for Planck mass PBHs. This is particularly noteworthy, as charged, stable relics like these could comprise all of the universe's dark matter.

The complexity of modeling the mass distribution in strong galaxy-scale gravitational lenses is becoming increasingly challenging. The latest imaging data, boasting high resolution and depth, have made it difficult for straightforward analytical methods to accurately depict the diverse lens structures spanning various spatial and mass scales. In response, we've developed an innovative, multi-scale technique based on wavelets to tackle this issue. This novel approach was tested using simulated Hubble Space Telescope data, containing distinct mass substructures, such as a small dark matter subhalo, a random field representing a population of non-localized subhalos, and galaxy-scale multipoles disrupting elliptical symmetry. The wavelet method successfully captured these intricate structures, enabled by the utilization of optimization techniques informed by gradients, automatic differentiation, and a vast parameter space. This hybrid framework seamlessly integrates analytical and pixel-based modeling with machine-learning optimizations, making it well-suited for fast, large-scale lens analysis. The accompanying code package, Herculens, has been made publicly available.

This work investigates how variations in the ratio of shear viscosity to entropy density ($\eta/s$) impact hydrodynamic simulations when its dependence on net baryochemical potential changes is taken into account. Prior studies mainly examined how temperature affects $ \eta /s $ or assumed it remains constant. This study explores the qualitative effect of a generalized $\eta/s(T, \mu_B)$ in a hybrid approach that combines a hadronic transport model with a 3+1 dimensional hydrodynamic code. To minimize bias caused by different equations of state, the ratio $\eta/s$ is directly parameterized using energy density and net baryon number density, adhering to hadronic transport and pQCD constraints. We evaluate how density dependence influences observables across various system sizes and energies in the RHIC-BES region and compare them to experimental results. We find that explicit density dependence has little effect on elliptic flow at RHIC-BES and only significant impact early in the collision process. Our results suggest that this parameterization can effectively model shear viscosity during hadronic transport in non-equilibrium scenarios.

The effect of a transversely polarized proton target on momentum-weighted Sivers asymmetries in various processes has been examined. The momentum-weighted Sivers asymmetries, particularly in SIDIS and Drell-Yan, were studied and found to result from the combination of TMD PDFs and FFs. Numerical calculations were carried out at COMPASS kinematics using existing parameterizations for the Sivers function, proton, pion and charged hadron unpolarized PDFs and FF. The resulting predictions show agreement with recent COMPASS data for SIDIS but highlight the need for more precise data from Drell-Yan to validate sign changes in the Sivers function.

Helium-3 is now considered one of the primary candidates for research in multiple disciplines including fundamental physics, atomic structure, magnetometry, metrology, chemistry, and medicine. In particular, studies have suggested that helium-3 nuclear magnetic resonance probes have the potential to become a new standard for measuring absolute magnetism. To establish this standard, a precise value of the helium-3 nuclear magnetic moment is necessary, however, its value has been estimated only indirectly and with moderate accuracy so far. In this investigation, we measured the ground-state hyperfine structure of the $^3$He$^+$ ion in a Penning trap to determine its nuclear $g$-factor and zero-field hyperfine splitting. Our results also allowed us to calculate the $g$-factor of the bare $^3$He nucleus and the diamagnetic shielding constant, which in turn, enabled the direct calibration of helium-3 NMR probes for the first time. Our measurements also significantly improved the accuracy of the zero-field hyperfine splitting and the Zemach radius compared to previous studies.

The accelerated failure time (AFT) model assumes a log-linear relationship between failure times and the covariates they are related to, making the covariate effects directly interpretable in terms of failure times. Unlike models that rely on hazard functions, AFT models are flexible and robust when their error distribution is not precisely known. However, AFT models typically assume linear predictors for the mean, with limited research addressing non-linear predictor scenarios. Recently, deep neural networks (DNNs) have gained attention due to their non-linear capabilities and ability to handle complex data patterns. By leveraging DNNs, we introduce a new AFT model called DeepR-AFT, which uses a combination of Gehan-type loss and a sub-sampling technique. Our simulation study reveals that DeepR-AFT significantly outperforms its parametric or semiparametric counterparts when predictor non-linearity is involved, while showing improved performance for large covariate dimensions in linear predictor scenarios. The proposed model's efficiency is further demonstrated through real-world dataset applications.

The Gaia Data Release 3 offers a comprehensive set of new data products to the community.
These data products are primarily astrophysical parameters produced by the Apsis system within the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium. 
This paper will provide a detailed overview of the contents of the astrophysical parameters in the Gaia Data Release 3 and describe their production method. 
Using mean spectra from the RVS, mean photometric and astrometric data, we derived a set of crucial parameters in Apsis for approximately 1.6 billion sources, 
including classification probabilities, source interstellar medium properties and distance information up to 470 million sources, 
along with a 2D map illustrating total galactic extinction and an analysis of 50 million sources through unsupervised classification. 
In addition to this information, we derived a large collection of stellar parameters for approximately 470 million sources, 
comprising Teff, mass, chemical abundances and ages among many other crucial parameters. 
This dataset represents the most comprehensive collection of astrophysical parameters to date, 
based uniquely on the Gaia dataset, which offers a valuable resource for astronomers worldwide.

We examine the weak universality of a two-dimensional nonlinear wave equation, specifically how it behaves with increasing fractional power. We first establish criteria for a sequence of Hamiltonians that converge to the $\Phi_2^4$ potential. Our criteria determine when these Hamiltonians' corresponding dynamics will eventually behave like a cubic wave equation, regardless of the nonlinearity's degree. Our research extends the work of Gubinelli-Koch-Oh by showing this is possible even when we don't have a solid understanding of how these dynamics behave close up with very strong nonlinearity.

Top Two algorithms emerged as an extension of Thompson sampling, designed to efficiently identify the best performing option in complex decision-making scenarios, for cases involving families of possible outcomes. By alternating between a leader and a challenger, the algorithms make probabilistic choices to determine the next option to consider. Despite showing promising real-world performance, theoretical evidence supporting Top Two methods was initially only available for scenarios involving normally distributed outcomes. In this paper, we develop a comprehensive analysis of the Top Two approach, highlighting beneficial characteristics of the leader, the challenger, and the distribution of possible outcomes. Our analysis yields Top Two algorithms with theoretical backing for scenarios involving distributions with bounded outcomes. Our proof technique also illustrates that the method used to select the leader can be replaced by alternative strategies, such as choosing the top-performing option based on observed results.

We introduce a relativistic spin density matrix theory for vector mesons using Kadanoff-Baym equations within a closed-time-path framework. This framework solidifies the calculation of spin-related variables like $\rho_{00}$ for vector mesons. By formulating $\rho_{00}$ for the $\phi$ meson, we express it in a factorizable form, decoupling momentum and spatial-time variables. Notably, we suggest that the dominant contribution to $\rho_{00}$ at lower energies originates from the $\phi$ fields that induce identical polarization on strange quark and antiquark pairs, analogous to electromagnetic field effects. Crucially, we observe that the $\phi$ meson's wave function reveals correlations between quark and antiquark polarizations facilitated by $\phi$ fields. This internal correlation leads to contributions of $\rho_{00}$ expressed as the square of non-vanishing fields that fluctuate significantly across space-time. These fluctuations in the strong force fields can be extracted from $\rho_{00}$ of quarkonium vector mesons to uncover fundamental properties of quantum chromodynamics.

To create powerful sequential recommenders, several methods have been introduced that learn representations of user behaviors through sequence modeling. Most existing approaches heavily rely on explicit item IDs, which, though somewhat effective, pose a challenge in transferring these methods to new recommendation contexts. This issue is addressed by introducing a novel universal sequence learning method called UniSRec. This approach utilizes the associated item description text to generate transferable representations across different recommendation settings. To achieve this, we developed a lightweight architecture combining parametric whitening and mixture-of-experts enhanced adaptors for universal item representation. Moreover, we incorporated two contrastive pre-training tasks, which involve sampling negatives from multiple domains, for universal sequence representation. Our method enables efficient transfer to new recommendation domains and platforms under both inductive and transductive settings, yielding promising results as evidenced by our extensive experiments on real-world datasets. Furthermore, we observed a notable performance improvement in cross-platform settings, highlighting the strong transferability of UniSRec. The code and pre-trained model for our method are publicly available on GitHub.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are frequently applied in data analysis, integrating graph information to achieve this. Despite their popularity, research has mainly focused on GNN's capabilities for tasks performed on entire graphs rather than at the individual node level, which involves tasks such as node classification - interpolating missing labels from existing ones. This study addresses this knowledge gap by examining GNN's capabilities for node-level tasks, which can be framed as a function interpolation problem. In particular, we establish the minimum weights and layers required for a GNN to approximate a band-limited function in d-dimensional space, revealing an improvement over fully connected neural networks in this context - specifically, our model uses a significantly smaller number of $O((\log \epsilon^{-1})^{d})$ weights when trained on $O((\log \epsilon^{-1})^{d})$ samples to achieve $\epsilon$-approximation for a discretized band-limited signal in d-dimensional space. This breakthrough is possible by connecting GNN's architecture to sampling theorems, making this research a pioneering effort in this field.

Many sequential data types have disparate lengths, with some sequences extending extensively. To model such long-range interactions effectively, we require neural attention mechanisms that can adapt to varying sequence lengths. Currently, existing attention models are limited in their ability to process lengthy sequences and typically rely on segmentation or padding to enforce uniform input lengths. To address this issue, we present a novel building block called ChordMixer, which is capable of modeling attention for sequences of diverse lengths. The proposed architecture comprises a position-wise transformation layer and an element-wise multi-layer perceptron (MLP), allowing repeated applications to yield a robust network backbone that efficiently combines input signals with their corresponding targets. Experimental results, which include the synthetic adding problem, long document classification, and DNA sequence-based taxonomy classification, demonstrate that ChordMixer outperforms other attention-based models significantly.

Achieving domain generalization, where models can adapt to new unseen domains,
hinges on developing domain-invariant feature representations that capture the core
semantics of object categories. Recent progress in weakly supervised vision-language
models has shown promise in capturing object characteristics through noisy text
annotations. However, the cost of annotating text for multiple source domains makes
this process infeasible. We aim to overcome this limitation by exploring the potential
of pre-trained multimodal networks as a resource to boost generalization. We present
INDIGO, a method that combines intrinsic modality from these networks with visual
information to enhance test-time generalization. Through experiments in various
domain generalization settings, we achieve state-of-the-art performance and offer a
detailed analysis of INDIGO.

Current navigation systems heavily rely on standalone inertial sensors for accurate positioning, particularly in situations with limited external data availability. In cases of data loss, inertial navigation performance tends to decline over time due to instrumental noise from low-cost sensors. Model-based estimation methods are commonly used to reduce noise and enhance meaningful information in navigation systems. However, guaranteeing optimal performance with model-based methods can be difficult due to variations in sensor quality, noise modeling, and calibration precision. Most existing inertial denoising models are based on conventional model-based methods, although data-driven approaches have been proposed in recent studies, particularly for denoising gyroscope measurements. The denoising task for accelerometer measurements is more complex due to unknown gravity projections on accelerometer axes. To address this challenge, we introduce multiple learning-based methods for accelerometer denoising and evaluate their performance against prominent denoising algorithms using both noise removal and stationary alignment tasks. The results of field experiments demonstrate that learning-based models outperform traditional filtering methods; a non-parametric kNN algorithm excels over state-of-the-art deep learning models; and denoising can significantly improve inertial signal reconstruction as well as navigation tasks by reducing errors up to one order of magnitude.

We have investigated the effects of strong gravitational lensing around rotating black holes in various gravitational theories by calculating the deflection angles. Our analysis indicates that rotating black holes in modified gravity and general relativity show greater disparities in image positioning and separation for SgrA* compared to M87*, but the time delays differ less for SgrA* compared to M87*. These findings can be used to differentiate between the two theories. Furthermore, we have also examined the shadow observables of various rotating black holes. Utilizing observations of M87* and SgrA* from the EHT, we have derived constraints for the MOG parameter. Specifically, we have determined the ranges of alpha values corresponding to black hole spins and established a new upper limit of 0.485 to 0.162.

This examination looks into multinomial coefficients and their recurrence relations within the context of generalized quantum deformed algebras. Furthermore, we establish and derive $\mathcal{R}(p,q)$- deformed multinomial probability distributions, both the standard and the negative forms. The relevant recurrence relations are also resolved and deduced. Furthermore, we derived results corresponding to specific quantum algebras found in literature.

Following the discovery of superconductive twisted bilayer graphene, which pioneered the field of twistronics, research has consistently unveiled captivating properties in moiré systems. In boron nitride twisted bilayers, we found that a given moiré periodicity corresponds to five distinct stackings that retain the hexagonal symmetry of the individual monolayers, contradicting the commonly discussed two configurations. To address this, we introduce a clear nomenclature and definitions that uniquely define the twist angle and stacking arrangement in hexagonal bilayers with threefold rotation symmetry. Furthermore, we utilize density functional theory to analyze the evolution of the band structure as a function of the twist angle for each of the five stacking sequences in boron nitride bilayers, revealing an indirect gap in all configurations and identifying characteristics that are conserved across the same stacking sequence regardless of the twist angle.

Deep learning model interpretability typically revolves around how the predicted outcome changes in response to input variations, using methods that often involve gradients. Some approaches aim to explain the logic behind each prediction in a way that doesn't rely on specific models. This paper makes the case for incorporating the way model parameters interact with inputs, proposing an improved interpretability technique that incorporates insights from multiple scaled inputs. The method introduced, "geometrically-guided integrated gradients," enhances the conventional integrated gradient technique by capturing the most informative attributions for each input. The authors demonstrate through extensive testing that this method performs better than its predecessors in subjective and quantitative assessments, also introducing a "model perturbation" validation method that pairs well with the standard "model randomization" check.

Significant advancements in the application of fluorescence angiography in reducing anastomotic leaks are hindered by subjective interpretation of the fluorescent signal among surgeons, resulting in variability in the technique's application. To overcome this challenge, we sought to develop a sophisticated artificial intelligence-powered algorithm that can accurately classify colonic tissue as either adequately perfused or not based on real-time data from intraoperative fluorescence angiography.

A classification model using the Resnet architecture was designed, trained, and validated using a comprehensive dataset of fluorescence angiography videos from colorectal resections. This model used images of both fluorescent and non-fluorescent tissue segments from patients, while validation utilized frames from patients not initially used for training. Both internal equipment data and external data from different cameras were employed to ensure broad applicability of the algorithm. We employed various metrics to gauge the model's performance, created saliency maps to visualize its outputs, and identified an optimal decision boundary.

A convolutional neural network model achieved a notable degree of success in classifying 1790 frames from 7 patients, with validation performed using 24 frames from 14 patients. Notably, the model achieved 100% accuracy on the initial dataset, while maintaining respectable performance of 80% on the validation dataset, with excellent precision of 100% on the initial dataset, though lower, though respectable recall rates of 68.8% on the validation dataset.

Automated analysis and classification of intraoperative fluorescence angiography data achieved a remarkably high degree of accuracy, thus empowering the standardized application of this valuable diagnostic tool. Furthermore, a web-based platform for the algorithm has been successfully developed.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) show great promise for food image recognition due to their ability to learn distinct visual patterns. However, accurately identifying distorted images poses a challenge for existing CNN models. To overcome this issue, a research team proposed a general specialist approach to develop a resilient ensemble model that can learn from clean images and become proficient in classifying images with various levels of distortion. This approach, combined with data augmentation and snapshot ensembling, allows each model in the ensemble to acquire specialized expertise in handling different types of distortions while retaining general skills for clean images. As a result, when filter outputs from the diverse experts are merged, it leads to enhanced classification accuracy. Fortunately, the learning process is not only effective but also efficient, as it requires only a single training process compatible with various supervised CNN models for transfer learning. Experimental studies conducted on several real-world databases have demonstrated a substantial improvement in classifying distorted images without compromising performance on clean images.

We introduce an efficient algorithm for assessing the predictive risks associated with Bayesian methods for various objective functions. This algorithm relies on the posterior covariance to yield estimators of the Gibbs and plugin generalization errors. Furthermore, we establish theoretical foundations that bridge the widely applicable information criterion, Bayesian sensitivity analysis, and infinitesimal jackknife approximation of Bayesian leave-one-out cross validation. In addition, we discuss the relevance of this approach to differentially-private learning scenarios.

We're examining specific linear differential operators on R^d with positive-definite symbols. Each operator Λ, defined by a symbol P, gives rise to a semigroup $e^{-t\Lambda}$ for t > 0, along with a convolution kernel $H^t_P$. Notably, the large-time behavior of $H^t_P(0)$ cannot be inferred from basic scaling arguments. By way of example, consider a simple case with the symbol $P(\xi) = (\eta+\zeta^2)^2+\eta^4$ in R^2. To gain insight, we've developed a method for analyzing large-time asymptotics for several classes of such examples, including how they are preserved under certain types of perturbations. For the specified P, we find $H^t_P(0)$ grows as $c_Pt^{-5/8}$ as t approaches infinity. Moreover, we demonstrate how these results contribute to understanding the convolution powers of complex functions on Z^d, laying a foundation for future research into semigroups associated with these operators, with identifying meaningful bounds for $H^t_P$ at large remaining an intriguing challenge.

We've found evidence that in some highly controlled systems, even those considered ideal or predictable, the efficient transport of spin properties through space can still be rare and doesn't always occur exactly as expected. By closely examining how a chain of spins with weakening interaction over longer distances affects their behavior over extended periods, we identified specific conditions that allow for nearly efficient transport and stable spin properties which do not diminish for thousands of spin interactions. Our findings were achieved through an analysis of spin patterns over time, the flow of spin information, the examination of specific physical operators involved in this transport, and by studying the conserved quantities. Interestingly, these conclusions provide a smooth connection to two well-known models that exhibit completely efficient transport: the basic model of particle movement and a highly balanced model.

This study defines LieYRep pairs and their properties by introducing their cohomology theory. We derive linear deformations using the second cohomology group. In addition, we define and analyze the characteristics of relative Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures on these pairs and their compatibility under certain conditions. Furthermore, we explore and demonstrate the relationship between $r$-matrix-Nijenhuis structures and Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures on Lie-Yamaguti algebras.

Modal logic can convey first-order conditions within the context of Kripke frames. Building upon Henrik Sahlqvist's pioneering work, a particular subset of modal formulas can have their corresponding first-order conditions identified through a systematic process. Researchers have successfully adapted this approach to increasingly intricate modal languages. In this study, we follow a similar approach and establish a correspondence theorem akin to Sahlqvist's work for Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL). A widely utilized formal language, LTL expands on basic modal logic by incorporating specific temporal operators such as Next (X) and Until (U). As a result, the class of formulas with corresponding first-order conditions becomes more complex. We identify a significant subset of LTL formulas comprising modal operators F, G, X, and U, and demonstrate the existence of a correspondence between these formulas and frame conditions expressible in the first-order language.

The Structure-from-Motion technique for recovering 3D scene structures often fails when encountering duplicate scene features that resemble one another visually. Most studies addressing this problem incorporate supplementary constraints, infer camera pose relationships from individual images, or examine geometries. However, this study presents a new method for using contextual scene information - local regions' spatial relationships - to guide the 3D scene reconstruction. We propose the concept of "track-communities" where groups of image tracks, representing distinct scene segments, are identified. Community detection is applied to segment the scene and detect ambiguities among segments. Tracks' neighboring information is analyzed to correct for inconsistencies, and partial 3D models are reconstructed from individual segments. Alignment of the partial models is performed with a cost function considering both 3D scene correspondences and camera pose relationships. Our approach is shown to efficiently handle duplicate scene features and accurately combine the partial models.

To address the issue of biased datasets in deep learning, particularly when models rely on incorrect features for decision-making, we introduce an innovative approach focusing on image classification. This approach allows users to guide a model's attention to specific image regions by simply clicking on areas of interest, thereby reducing the effect of co-occurrence bias and enhancing model transferability and interpretability. Unlike existing methods that require extensive pixel-level annotations, our approach presents a new interactive system, coupled with an efficient active learning strategy to minimize the number of annotations needed. Through a combination of numerical analysis and user testing, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed system, comparing favorably to existing methods that often rely on expensive polygon-based segmentation masks. The results show that our approach saves significant time and resources, delivering improved performance even when the dataset is heavily biased. The experiments also confirm the efficiency, reasonableness, and reliability of our proposed system.

Our Hyper-pool algorithm combines individual trip requests to create highly attractive shared rides with high occupancy rates. This innovation builds upon our previous ExMAS ride-pooling method by introducing two new algorithms to further group similar rides into compact, stop-to-stop journeys. Each of these journeys features a single pick-up and drop-off point optimal for all passengers involved. By grouping these compact rides together, our algorithm generates hyper-pooled rides that are comparable to public transportation. Our framework starts at a low level of pooling, allowing us to gradually increase it to ensure the resulting rides remain attractive even at higher aggregation levels. This results in a set of highly attractive pooled rides per travel service variant. Our algorithms, available for public use, can be applied to real-world datasets and have the potential to unlock the full benefits of ride-pooling. In a test using travel data from Amsterdam, we successfully combined over 220 passengers into 40 highly compact hyper-pooled rides with an average occupancy of nearly six people per vehicle.

To expedite the neural architecture search process, strategies that minimize training time are crucial. This necessitates the use of performance estimation techniques. The effectiveness of these methods varies based on their precision, adaptability, and processing speed. This research presents EmProx Score, an innovative approach that leverages an encoder-decoder framework to transform candidate architectures into continuous embeddings. The performance of candidates is then estimated via weighted kNN based on the known architectures' embedding vectors. EmProx Score achieves performance estimates comparable to MLP, yet it is nearly nine times faster to train than NAO. Benchmarking EmProx Score against existing methods demonstrates comparable or superior accuracy, with training times that are five to eighty times faster.

Recent federated learning research suggests using large batches significantly enhances convergence speeds but incurs a greater computational expense than smaller batches. To counterbalance this drawback, we have developed FedAMD, a comprehensive framework that partitions participating nodes into distinct anchor and miner groups, dynamically allocating them probabilities over time. Each node in the anchor group calculates gradients with large batches, viewed as a reference point. In contrast, nodes within the miner group execute a sequence of local updates using sequential small batches and adhere to an optimized path toward the global minimum, as informed by the aggregated reference points from the anchor group. Through $\epsilon$-approximation, FedAMD displays a superior convergence rate of $O(1/\epsilon)$ in non-convex objectives with constant anchor sampling, significantly outperforming existing BVR-L-SGD at $O(1/\epsilon^{3/2})$. Additionally, FedAMD reduces the communication overhead by $O(1/\epsilon)$ in comparison. Real-world datasets showcase the potency of our algorithm, solidifying its supremacy over the existing BVR-L-SGD approach.

Quality indicators, such as passive voice and sentence length, are often used to assess the quality of natural language requirements in research and practice. However, a comprehensive understanding of quality factors is still missing within the research community. This gap affects not only the effective utilization of existing quality factors but also their continuous improvement. In order to bridge this knowledge gap, we propose the creation of a comprehensive ontology that structures quality factors for textual requirements, making them easily accessible and usable to everyone. Our initial effort consists of applying a systematic approach to analyze 105 primary studies and develop the first version of this ontology. We are eager to share it and welcome fellow researchers to join a collaborative community effort to build upon and maintain this knowledge repository, ensuring that it accurately represents the community's consensus, promotes consistent reporting, and serves as a central hub for the existing body of knowledge on quality factors.

We investigate the significance of particle and lepton mass effects in the multi-body decay $H \rightarrow Z^*(\rightarrow \tau^+\tau^-) + Z^*(\rightarrow \tau^+\tau^-)$. Since the problem's scale is defined by the off-shell gauge boson masses, $p_a^2$ and $p_b^2$, rather than $m_H^2$, mass effects from tau leptons are substantial, particularly in decays near threshold. Our study evaluates and compares the rates and single-angle decay distributions of this identical-particle decay scenario with the rates and single-angle decay distributions of a distinct particle decay scenario, $H \rightarrow Z^*(\rightarrow e^+e^-) + Z^*(\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-)$, where lepton masses are negligible.

The third data release of the Gaia dataset offers significant new opportunities for researchers in the field of astronomy, thanks to a comprehensive collection of astrophysical parameters for over 500 million stars. Our research showcases the high quality and versatility of these data products in multiple astrophysical contexts. To that end, we have utilized the data from the Gaia catalogue and cross-referenced it with external datasets to produce six distinct samples of stars with reliable astrophysical parameters. Our analysis initially concentrates on three broad samples spanning the range from young and massive stars to ultracompact dwarfs. These samples are accompanied by supplemental information which can be accessed through the Gaia database. Our research further identifies approximately 15,740 confirmed carbon stars and 5,863 stars resembling the Sun, as well as providing a unified dataset of parameters for a group of reference stars known as the Spectro-Photometric Standards. Additionally, we have utilized the data to explore several applications including: analysing the rotation curve of the Milky Way, studying planetary systems, determining the ages of unseen companions to certain stars and simulating the apparent colours of the Sun in different spectral bands.

FLASH radiotherapy has garnered attention in several preclinical cancer research studies, due to its high dose rate during irradiation. However, there is currently no real-time dosimeter capable of tracking the dosage delivered. In this work, a beam current transformer was developed, encompassing selection of the ferromagnetic core and shielding, in conjunction with a low-noise front-end electronics circuit to enhance its detection capabilities. The transformer prototype has the capacity to monitor a beam current range from 1.2 micro-amperes to 200 milliamperes, characterized by a sub-20 nanosecond rise time and a signal loss rate of under 0.05% per microsecond. Initial on-site measurements were also carried out. Our goal is to integrate the BCT with an ionisation chamber to continuously monitor beam current, shape, and position, creating a reliable real-time dosing system.

A new method for single-channel partial wave analysis, driven by energy dependency, has been developed. This approach bypasses the need for complex theoretical models of two-body reactions by utilizing key properties of analyticity instead. Traditional methods for determining energy-dependent partial waves and multipoles required creating a theoretical model, solving it, fitting free parameters, and reconstructing partial wave amplitudes. To eliminate the necessity for constructing and solving elaborate models, researchers suggest decomposing the partial waves in Laurent form, expanding the regular component in a rapid converging series using Pietarinen's conformal variable. Then, they fit the parameters – consisting of pole parameters and Pietarinen coefficients – to an extensive collection of reaction data. Due to a clear understanding of the reaction's singularities (poles and branch points), the complexity associated with the theoretical model is minimized. A particular implementation of this approach has been proposed for K-Lambda photo-production, leveraging an established data set. Nonetheless, difficulties arise from a complicated formalism and a large number of fitting parameters. To address this issue, simplifications of the analytic structure are implemented in conjunction with the amplitude+partial wave analysis (AA/PWA) method for K-Lambda photoproduction. To manage computational requirements, simplifications of the expansion's analytic structure are also necessary.

Fermi J1544-0649, a transient GeV source, was initially discovered during a GeV flare in 2017, showing characteristics of a blazar at multi-wavelength observations. Between flare events, this source appears to resemble a normal galaxy. The detection of broad absorption lines further supports the investigation into the'misaligned blazar scenario.' We examined Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) and East Asian VLBI Network (EAVN) data from 2018-2020, discovering four jet components from Fermi J1544-0649, with a viewing angle ranging from 3.7 degrees to 7.4 degrees. The lower angle suggests that the gamma-ray emission from this blazar has a very low duty cycle, while the upper angle is in line with the'misaligned blazar scenario.' Following the discovery in 2018, further multi-wavelength observations found that the source remains dormant in GeV, X-ray, and optical bands. Additionally, neutrino analysis revealed a significant excess.

Semi-supervised learning is an essential approach to reducing the reliance of machine learning models on labeled data. This method has shown effectiveness in handling structured data like images and language, using techniques such as pre-trained models and data augmentation. However, these approaches may not be applicable to data without known domain structures. Pseudo-labeling (PL) methods are simpler but prone to issues with noisy samples and arbitrary assignment thresholds that are difficult to set. This paper overcomes these challenges with a new technique called Confident Sinkhorn Allocation (CSA), which prioritizes accurate labeling of highly confident samples and uses optimal transport to determine the best allocation. CSA achieves better results than the current leading methods in semi-supervised learning. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/amzn/confident-sinkhorn-allocation.

We introduce a new expression, $\zeta^k(s)$, and conditionally prove the main term of its related correlation sum under specific distribution and congruence assumptions. This is then applied to derive the asymptotics for the correlation sum of the divisor function $\tau_3(n)$ for any composite shift. The results from our elementary method, involving the delta-method, are verified to match those of prior calculations based on probabilistic arguments. The approach we present is also general, extending the main term computation for various correlations of the divisor function, such as $\sum_{n\le X} \tau_k(n) f(n+h)$, and can potentially be applied to any arithmetic function, $f(n)$.

We present a theoretical approach to induce photon emission from a vacuum state by periodically altering a quantum system, indirectly linked to the cavity through a mediating quantum system. For the most basic case, this is done using a 2-level atom with adjustable properties (a "t-qubit"), which is connected via weak magnetic forces to both the cavity and an additional quantum system ("ancilla qubit"). Under specific resonance conditions, our findings suggest that the ground state can give rise to highly interconnected quantum states involving few photons when adjustments are made based on system characteristics, including the t-qubit's inherent and adjustable properties. This phenomenon, previously predicted using simplified equations, also holds under various real-world dissipation scenarios and is verified by computational simulations.

Neural networks with quantized weights have garnered significant interest for their reduced space and computation complexity during inference, and some have suggested they act as implicit regularizers improving generalizability. Although this notion has been discussed, no prior study has formally investigated its validity. In this paper, we examine binary neural networks as stochastic processes, tracking distribution propagation across different layers, and develop a new model, a neural network with continuous parameters, to approximate this propagation. By analyzing the neural tangent kernel, we demonstrate its eigenvalues decrease exponentially, akin to a randomized Gaussian kernel, indicating the binary neural network can only represent a subset of functions compared to its real-weight counterpart.
