When it comes to Einstein gravity and a zero cosmological constant, there is no precise equilibrium point with a horizon. However, for high temperatures, the portion of the Euclidean diamond contained by the boundary acts as an approximate equilibrium point with the saddle's horizon converging with the boundary. This high-temperature partition function helps explain the recent calculation by Banks, Draper and Farkas, where the entropy of causal diamonds was derived from the boundary term in the Euclidean action. Conversely, when considering a positive cosmological constant or Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity with or without a cosmological constant, there exists a precise equilibrium point with a finite boundary temperature, where the causal diamond is defined by the equilibrium point rather than pre-determined.

A novel coinless quantisation method is applied to both continuous and discrete-time Birth and Death processes, resulting in the derivation of a quantum Hamiltonian from the matrix representing the Birth and Death equation using the square root of its stationary distribution. This quantum model exhibits eigenvalue and eigenvector relationships mirroring its classical counterpart. When Birth and Death rates are chosen according to the coefficients of Askey's orthogonal polynomial equations, the resulting quantum system becomes exactly solvable. Specifically, its eigenvectors coincide with the polynomials themselves, and eigenvalues can be computed analytically. Many periodic instances emerge, characterised by integer eigenvalues, particularly when integer parameters are involved. This parallels exactly solvable quantum mechanical systems. These exactly solvable Markov chains offer the versatility of multiple adjustable parameters, facilitating simulations in diverse applications.

A specific matrix known as a frequency rectangle of type FR(m, n; q), is an m x n grid that meets specific conditions where each symbol from a set of size q occurs in each row a certain number of times and in each column another specific number of times. Given these conditions, if two of these frequency rectangles, of the same type, are combined, each pair of symbols appears the same number of times. If all possible pairs of these frequency rectangles meet these conditions, then they are considered a set of mutually orthogonal frequency rectangles, which can be denoted by k-MOFR(m, n; q). Research demonstrates the equivalence of a specific case of these frequency rectangles, a  k-MOFR(2, 2n; 2), to another specific matrix known as an orthogonal array, an OA(2n, k, 2, 2), and also proves that the existence of one of these matrices implies the existence of another specific case of these frequency rectangles, a k-MOFR(2m, 2n; 2). Further, under certain conditions a specific case of these frequency rectangles, a  k-MOFR(4, 2a; 2), can be constructed, using an additional matrix known as a Hadamard matrix, of a specific order. Additionally, these frequency rectangles can be categorized further based on a specific condition. They can be called t-orthogonal, if, under this new condition, each subset, of a specific size t, contains a specific arrangement of entries, a specific number of times. Research demonstrates the equivalence of these frequency rectangles, under this new condition, to another type of matrix known as t-independent vectors over a specific finite field. Research also demonstrates the relationship between these frequency rectangles, under this new condition, and other specific conditions on these vectors, as well as provides an example, using an odd prime, of how a specific case of these frequency rectangles, a  k-MOFR(n; 2), can be used to improve the lower bounds of previously known results for this case.

A fundamental mathematical relationship is established for how disclination lines move within nematic liquid crystals in relation to their $\mathbf{Q}$ tensor properties. Unlike other factors that become unstable near their centers of defect, the $\mathbf{Q}$ tensor remains stable throughout. Building on existing work, the core of the disclination line is defined as the point where its uniaxial and biaxial properties converge or the two highest $\mathbf{Q}$ eigenvalues intersect. This allows for a precise formula that describes how fast a line moves in relation to spatial and time-dependent variations of $\mathbf{Q}$ on that line. An approximate linear expression for $\mathbf{Q}$ is applied to provide analytical solutions for various configurations, including interacting lines, loops, responses to external influences, and shear flows, with the observed behaviors tied to their topological or geometric properties. Calculations from this mathematical model align with three-dimensional numerical results based on a free energy function allowing anisotropic elastic responses.

A coinless quantisation approach for reversible Markov chains on networks is introduced. A quantum Hamiltonian is derived from the fundamental transition matrix by applying a similarity transformation, utilizing the square root of the reversible distribution. The classical and quantum evolution of these chains is described by solving the eigenvalue equation of the derived Hamiltonian. Approximately twenty Markov chains that have exactly solvable cases, based on the hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials in the Askey scheme derived by Odake-Sasaki, are proposed for investigating the quantum-classical dichotomy. Five illustrative examples are given to demonstrate the calculations, each related to specific cases such as the Krawtchouk, Hahn, q-Hahn, Charlier and Meixner.

Drawing inspiration from the recently solved black hole information paradox, this note proposes an analogy to infer the key parameter governing the state of consciousness. The concept of the Page curve and the associated Page time serve as the foundation. Crucially, the interconnection between the brain's state and the pattern of neuronal activity over time, as well as the interconnectedness of brain networks that defy strict separation, are pivotal in this hypothesis.

It's been established that pure entanglement in mixed states cannot be created through certain types of operations for specific dimension combinations, but it is possible in other cases with the right methods and dimensions. In particular, it has been found that pure entanglement can be distilled using specific types of operations from systems of dimension $2 \otimes 4$ or higher, given that certain conditions are met, and that in other cases, different operations are more effective. These discoveries include the ability to produce certain types of highly entangled tripartite systems.

Previous studies on large pretrained language models revealed a multitude of human-like biases towards various demographic groups, prompting an intense focus on developing methods to identify and quantify such biases, in hopes of creating benchmarks that could guide the creation of more effective bias-reducing techniques.  However, recent research has shown that current benchmarks are lacking in a strong experimental foundation, hindering the derivation of meaningful conclusions from the evaluation metrics they provide.  This study further emphasizes these concerns by pointing out the existing methods and benchmarks are plagued by inaccuracy and excessive experimental noise, severely restricting the insights that can be gleaned from evaluating language models based on these standards.  Consequently, this research introduces a novel approach for accurately measuring and quantifying the biases displayed by generative language models, and applies this framework to an in-depth examination of GPT-3's occupational gender bias, proposing specific prompting techniques for reducing these biases without the requirement of model retraining.

In conventional software development, Requirements Engineering activities have been thoroughly researched and established, but they become less effective in artificial intelligence-based software systems where the internal mechanisms are unclear. Current studies primarily explore utilizing AI to automate RE tasks, whereas research on requirements engineering for AI systems (RE4AI) remains limited. This study aims to investigate the methods for defining requirements for AI systems, identify existing frameworks, tools, and models for modeling requirements, and identify existing challenges in RE4AI. To achieve this goal, a systematic review of papers related to RE4AI approaches was conducted, and 43 primary studies were analyzed. The study's findings indicate several challenges in current RE4AI practices, highlighting the need for new tools and techniques that support AI system requirements engineering. Moreover, the results show that empirical research on RE4AI predominantly focuses on self-driving cars and data requirements management, whereas areas such as ethics, trust, and transparency remain under researched and require further investigation.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) is currently standardizing post-quantum cryptographic methods that can withstand both classical and quantum attacks. This manuscript offers an in-depth analysis and comparison of the latest BIKE QC-MDPC code-based post-quantum key exchange implementations, which are NIST standardization candidates. Evaluations consider software, hardware, and hybrid hardware-software configurations, focusing on their performance and hardware resource efficiency.

Following allegations of Twitter's liberal bias in its verification and moderation policies, Elon Musk, after acquiring the company, vowed to enhance free speech on the platform. This move raised concerns about a potential surge in influence of contentious figures, particularly those from the right. This article utilizes a publicly disclosed list of Twitter users who obtained the blue verified badge in 2022 to explore how Musk's takeover affected user engagement on the platform. Analyzing 4.9 million tweets from a subset of contentious accounts, it was found that the period after Musk's acquisition witnessed a significant rise in engagement on contentious posts, with no additional spike in engagement following verification. This outcome can be attributed to increased activity from a newly sympathetic user base.

We analyze the partition function of quantum gravity, focusing on a spatial region resembling a sphere, of fixed volume, to calculate the dimension of its Hilbert space in a leading approximation. The result reveals a relationship between this dimension and the entropy related to the boundary of this region. This entropy-based relationship is theoretically valid within the framework of effective field theory, as long as the region's boundary curvature singularity is smoothed over. This study expands upon an earlier, seminal computation performed by Gibbons and Hawking for a de Sitter spacetime volume, demonstrating that in confined spatial volumes, quantum gravity can be described using a holographic principle.

Let $K$ be a totally real field and $r\geq5$ a fixed rational prime. In this study, we apply a modified approach to the modular method developed by Freitas and Siksek, tailored for non-trivial, primitive solutions $(x,y,z)$ in $\mathcal{O}_K^3$ of the form $x^r+y^r=z^p$ (where $p$ varies), over totally real subfields of $K(\zeta_r)$. The approach is adapted from Freitas' work, specifically to handle the case of $K=\mathbb{Q}$ which yields no non-trivial, primitive integer solutions $(x,y,z)$ with $2|z$ for certain prime $r$ values and sufficiently large $p$. Similar findings are obtained for quadratic fields like $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, showing no non-trivial, primitive solutions $(x,y,z)\in\mathcal{O}_K^3$ with $\sqrt{2}|z$ for certain $r$ values and large enough $p$.

The advancements in deep neural networks have enabled significant breakthroughs in various domains like textual and relational representations, making it possible to explore relation extraction beyond traditional text-oriented methods. However, research into leveraging diverse domain information is still in its infancy, and models that effectively incorporate multiple information types are anticipated to make substantial contributions to problem-solving globally. Focusing on Drug-Drug Interactions as a case study, this thesis undertakes a study of relation extraction incorporating heterogeneous domain data. Firstly, a deep neural relation extraction model is developed and its attention mechanism is examined. Next, a technique is introduced to merge information about drug molecular structures and descriptions with text inputs to demonstrate the utility of this approach in the context of relation extraction. To further exploit heterogeneous data, a range of relevant items, such as proteins, medical terminology and pathways, are gathered from various existing databases and a knowledge graph (KG) is constructed to contain these items. By performing link prediction tasks on this constructed dataset, the model acquires representations of drugs that encompass the multiple domain data. Finally, a technique is developed to integrate the input sentence information with the constructed knowledge graph, resulting in a proposed model that significantly outperforms previous results when tested on a widely used dataset, thus highlighting the benefits of utilising diverse domain data in relation extraction tasks from literature.

Collaborative creativity involving both humans and AI can unlock full potential when the AI can engage in two-way communication. Most co-creative systems restrict themselves to receiving input from users only, preventing them from being perceived as genuine partners. An initial study with 38 participants found that enabling the AI to converse with humans boosts collaboration and user involvement. Results indicate users appreciate AI that interacts with them, viewing it as more trustworthy, personal, and intelligent. These findings underscore the need to consider potential pitfalls in human-AI collaboration, particularly as it grows more engaging. Moving forward, the authors employ participatory design fiction to address emerging ethical issues stemming from the interaction between humans and a communicative AI that co-creates.

The versatility and safety of soft robots make them ideal for manipulation tasks, but they're typically confined to a narrow hemispherical workspace due to their bidirectional design.  To expand this limitation, researchers designed and built an innovative soft robotic arm system, integrating a base-mounted prismatic actuator made from pneumatic artificial muscles and a piston, allowing it to be back-driven.  The addition of this actuator increased the manipulable volume by over 116%, enabling previously unattainable tasks like surface placement and container extraction.  The combination of a soft robotic arm with a prismatic joint significantly enhances the usability of soft robots for object manipulation, driving advancements in modular, human-centric soft robotic systems.

To utilize bosonic quanta in high-speed quantum information processing, rapidly cooling motional modes is a critical step. In this study, we aimed to minimize the time required for cooling, moving beyond the constraints of traditional sideband cooling methods. To achieve this, we developed a method utilizing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to expedite the process. The proposed scheme effectively accelerated motional cooling of a large magnonic sphere, with the potential for broader applications in more intricate systems. Most notably, our DRL approach allows for control of regimes that conventional methods cannot reach, including areas beyond the conventional rotating wave approximation. This development enables a comprehensive toolkit for rapidly creating macroscopic quantum states for use in quantum technologies.

This article delves into additional properties of the weighted numerical radius of a Hilbert space operator and utilizes the newly developed concept to derive novel inequalities, focusing on both the weighted numerical radius and the numerical radius itself. Notably, it establishes new relationships for the numerical radius and provides comparisons between the numerical radius and the real and imaginary parts. Furthermore, it explores and presents inequalities specifically tailored for sectorial operators.

This article exploits specific properties of the operator transformation
$\mathscr{C}_{M,m}(A) = (M\mathbf1_{\mathcal{H}} - A^*)(A-m\mathbf1_{\mathcal{H}})$
to establish new inequalities for the bounded linear operator $A$ on a complex
Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. Notably, new connections are derived between
the norms of $A$, $A^*$, the real and imaginary parts of $A$. Furthermore,
numerical radius inequalities are presented, extending existing known inequalities.

We propose a novel monocular visual odometry algorithm called EDS, 
utilizing both event and frame data. This algorithm leverages the event 
generation model to predict camera movement during periods of low illumination.
EDS employs a direct probabilistic approach, estimating brightness changes 
across pixels and comparing them against actual brightness events to calculate 
camera movement. This yields a semi-dense 3D map through photometric bundle 
adjustment. Notably, EDS is the first method to implement 6-DOF visual odometry 
directly using events and frames, effectively mitigating the drawbacks of indirect 
approaches caused by changing visual appearances. Furthermore, for a specified error 
threshold, EDS can function with lower frame rates than existing frame-based VO 
solutions. This has the potential to enable low-power motion-tracking applications 
where cameras are triggered selectively and our approach fills in the gaps. We make 
our code and dataset publicly available for further development and testing.

The ground state phase diagram of a specific spin model, namely, the dimerized spin-1/2 XX honeycomb model, with and without the influence of a transverse magnetic field is well understood. Without the external magnetic field, this system displays two distinct phases at its quantum ground state, namely, the Néel and the dimerized phases. Furthermore, when the magnetic field is applied, the canted Néel and paramagnetic phases emerge. Through this study, using a combination of precise numerical methods including Lanczos exact diagonalization and the Density matrix renormalization group, the quantum correlations and the relationships between nearby spins, as quantified by concurrence and quantum discord, are investigated. The results indicate that the quantum correlations successfully pinpoint the quantum critical points throughout the ground state phase diagram in agreement with existing findings. Moreover, concurrence and quantum discord, despite being indicators of short-range phenomena, can offer insight into long-ranged critical correlations in this system. The analysis also uncovers a notable "magnetic entanglement" phenomenon originating at a specific threshold value of the external magnetic field, corresponding to the point where all nearby spins become entangled.

Deep learning models used in computational imaging primarily focus on predicting a single reconstructed image, but in reality, these point estimates can be unreliable or inadequate due to ill-posedness, nonlinearity, and other issues. Bayesian methods, however, consider images and measurements as interlinked random variables, aiming to approximate the posterior distribution of unknown quantities. Recently, normalizing flows have been proposed as an alternative to traditional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, but they come with high memory and computational demands, and underperform on complex problems. To address these challenges, this work presents C-Trumpets, conditional injective flows engineered specifically for imaging applications, which reduce the computational and memory requirements while improving performance on various tasks like CT and nonlinear inverse scattering, and enable fast approximation of point estimates along with uncertainty quantification.

The choice of the ideal neural architecture for a specific machine learning task is heavily influenced by multiple factors, encompassing both the dataset's complexity and resource availability such as processing speed, computational power, and energy efficiency. The search for optimal neural architectures for tabular datasets, a significant yet understudied issue, is challenged by the fact that many existing approaches, designed for image-based problems, incorporate resource constraints into reinforcement learning protocols which sometimes lead to suboptimal results. In an effort to improve this, researchers developed TabNAS, a novel approach to efficiently handling resource constraints in neural architecture search on tabular datasets, by utilizing a reinforcement learning controller inspired by the concept of rejection sampling. TabNAS efficiently discards non-compliant architectures without further evaluation and incorporates a Monte-Carlo-based correction to the policy gradient updates to adapt to the filtering process. Experimental results on several datasets confirm that TabNAS outperforms previous methods in finding better, constraint-obeying models.

The given article enhances the triangle inequality for complex numbers by utilizing the Hermite-Hadamard inequality for convex functions, followed by the discussion of its practical applications to operator inequalities.

A simplified mathematical model is created to study complex phenomena in many-body quantum systems that interact with their environment. When this model is applied to a specific chain-like structure with various thermal configurations, it leads to the derivation of a mathematical equation that explains how the system reaches a state of thermal balance. Using another mathematical approach, equations are developed to describe how certain components of the system interact over time. These results enable the analysis of complex dynamics in a system that responds to various types of changes, such as fluctuations in temperature and external stimuli, while facilitating a deeper understanding of how different factors influence each other in the process. This model is designed for the investigation of temperature-dependent effects and their impact on quantum systems that undergo changes in response to external stimuli or temperatures.

In the context of two-dimensional gravity, we provide an in-depth and non-perturbative explanation of the chaotic phase in the quantum realm. We describe a non-perturbative framework, derived from the universe field theory associated with gravity, to accurately capture the behavior of the chaotic phase in the 2D gravity system. Guided by our theory, a flavor-matrix description of holographic gravity, which displays $\mathrm{U}(n|n)$ causal symmetry breaking and subsequent restoration. However, studies on JT gravity and its relatives alone cannot achieve causal symmetry through an action principle, yet their universe field theory, the Kodaira-Spencer theory, possesses this property. We then directly link our flavor-matrix theory with brane-antibrane correlators in the Kodaira-Spencer theory and demonstrate how causal symmetry breaking and restoration can be interpreted through topological D-brane vacua transitions. Furthermore, our findings reveal an open-closed string duality relationship between the holomorphic Chern-Simons theory and its closed-string counterpart, the Kodaira-Spencer theory of gravity. We aim to establish a connection between the geometric principles derived from this duality and the characteristic spectral patterns exhibited by the chaotic phase in the quantum realm.

When water droplets in clouds combine to form rain, it's often due to a process where smaller droplets merge to form larger ones. However, these droplets do not always stick together, as the air around them creates a cushioning effect, reducing the likelihood of merging. To better understand how this "sticking" rate occurs, researchers have developed new techniques to track and analyze the behavior of cloud droplets. They used advanced 3D tracking methods to study droplet pairs falling through still air with extremely high precision, which allowed them to study the exact movements and forces at play when droplets are just a short distance apart. This analysis revealed that droplets that do merge exhibit distinct movements, with forces exceeding a specific threshold value, which was discovered to be connected to the air's influence on their interactions. The research suggests that understanding the pattern of droplet movements within turbulent clouds may hold the key to determining the sticking rate, providing a fundamental understanding of the merging process.

Recent breakthroughs in NLP research have proven that pre-trained autoregressive models can accomplish numerous tasks through novel training paradigms involving little to no data examples. This research develops two highly advanced, GPT-like models with enormous parameter sizes trained on an extensive library spanning 60 languages from 25 distinct linguistic backgrounds, utilizing large databases to accelerate progress. These models are engineered to mimic GPT-3 architecture with GPT-2 sources, coupled with efficient training and inference protocols via Deepspeed and Megatron frameworks, effectively yielding models competitive with Facebook's recent XGLM models while expanding their language coverage to better assist resource-constrained regions and languages of CIS countries and Russia. This paper explains the design reasoning behind the models' architecture, delves into data preparation methods, fine-tunes the models by creating and testing smaller adaptations, chooses the optimal tokenization approach through thorough evaluation, assesses model performance across diverse multilingual tasks, including categorization, generation, sequence labeling, and knowledge-based probing. Additionally, these models are tested with zero- and few-shot learning methods, with further comparative analysis of their performance on categorization tasks relative to Facebook's cutting-edge multilingual model XGLM. All the developed source code, including the mGPT XL model, is now freely available.

We examine the Local Polynomial Interpolation-based Gradient Descent (LPI-GD) method, a recently proposed solution to empirical risk minimization problems, specifically for smooth and strongly convex loss functions with a given condition number. Assuming these loss functions are also H\"older continuous with respect to the data, our focus is on its performance in terms of oracle complexity, which is $\tilde{O}\left(\sigma m^d \log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$ for a specified accuracy. A notable improvement is observed when scaling the factor $m^d$, yielding $O((1/\varepsilon)^{d/2\eta})$. We also observe that LPI-GD offers a better oracle complexity than gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under certain parameter conditions. This study introduces accelerated LPI-GD methods for empirical risk minimization, achieving a more efficient oracle complexity of $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\sigma} m^d \log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, in addition to providing empirical validation through an initial investigation of local polynomial interpolation-based gradient methods, which shows promising results with accelerated LPI-GD performing better than its traditional counterparts in specific scenarios.

In this paper, a novel method is introduced to enhance particle filtering for systems with signals that change over time according to specific equations. The method involves converting continuous equations into discrete versions, which facilitates efficient filtering techniques in systems with high dimensions. To achieve this, the method is engineered to minimize exponential growth in computational complexity with increased system size, while the estimation errors remain relatively constant. The method's efficiency and effectiveness are demonstrated through simulations on the Lorenz 96 system with noisy parameters. Furthermore, the method provides a broader theoretical framework for filtering systems where the continuous dynamics are known but observations occur at distinct times. By leveraging this method, the marginal probability distributions of these discrete-time systems can converge to their original continuous counterparts, even under certain weak convergence schemes for discretisation.

The process by which interstellar dust particles are formed with varying sizes involves the collision of supernovae ejecta, stellar winds and stochastic acceleration, which leads to smaller grains being generated from shattered large ones. We developed a unique approach to study stochastic acceleration using a combined magnetohydrodynamic (MHD)-particle-in-cell (PIC) method integrated into the astrophysical fluid code RAMSES, representing dust particles as large ``superparticles'' and considering aerodynamic drag and Lorentz force on them. Our method was put through rigorous numerical testing in different physical environments to confirm its effectiveness, while illustrating possible grain acceleration mechanisms. We conducted an experiment simulating decaying dusty MHD turbulence with grain characteristics resembling grains found in cold neutral mediums and discovered that under typical conditions, these grains could achieve high velocities beyond their shattering limits. Our study shows that this occurs regardless of whether the grains are charged or neutral. Notably, while charged grains displayed higher gas-grain relative drift velocities, the shapes of the distributions suggest that the extra gas-grain interaction due to Lorentz force provides grains protection from shattering. Our simulations also highlight connections to naturally occurring $\mu$m-sized presolar grains which seem to have remained pristine throughout their lifetimes.
The Hybrid-AIM simulator, which has been employed in the research of Sharon and Stone (2017) and Parks-Young and Sharon (2022), is discussed in the following technical details.

We demonstrate the non-existence of odd-dimensional, stable, and compact minimal immersions within the product of two complex projective spaces. Furthermore, it is shown that the only stable, compact, and minimal immersions within the product of a quaternionic projective space and any other Riemannian manifold consist of products of quaternionic projective subspaces combined with stable, compact, and minimal immersions of the second manifold. These findings build upon earlier results for immersions of low dimensions or codimensions and extend them to cases involving arbitrary dimensions. Additionally, it is proven that the stable, compact, and minimal immersions within the product of an octonionic projective plane and any other Riemannian manifold solely comprise products of octonionic projective subspaces combined with stable, compact, and minimal immersions of the second manifold.

We consider an imaginary quadratic field denoted as $K$ and a prime $p$ that splits within $K$. This paper develops an anticyclotomic Euler system associated with an elliptic modular form's adjoint representation after a base change to $K$. Our work also connects this Euler system to a $p$-adic $L$-function that stems from Eischen-Wan's and Eischen-Harris-Li-Skinner's $p$-adic $L$-function constructions for unitary groups. The result is a proof of new cases of the Bloch-Kato conjecture in rank zero, along with progress toward a key divisibility in an Iwasawa main conjecture.

The challenge of active mapping focuses on planning an efficient series of observations with limited resources, such as a specified distance traveled. This paper explores active grid mapping using a range sensor like LiDAR or a depth camera. Existing methods optimize information-based measures linking occupancy grid probabilities to sensor readings. However, the computational complexity of ray tracing within a grid structure makes the optimization problem non-differentiable, which forces these methods to rely on discrete search spaces of possible trajectories. To address this, our research introduces a differentiable approximation of the information shared between a grid map and ray-based observations. This new formulation, which leverages gradient ascent optimization in the continuous space of possible sensor poses, yields more informative and obstacle-avoiding trajectories. Our method is evaluated through simulations and real-world experiments in various 2-D and 3-D environments.

Our objective is to uncover concealed motion in video sequences through amplification. This can be achieved via two primary methodologies: the Eulerian and Lagrangian approaches. The first method enhances motion by operating directly on video pixels, whereas the Lagrangian technique leverages optical flow analysis to analyze and amplify pixel paths. Identifying microexpressions, which are brief, localized facial movements, presents a significant challenge. In this research, we introduce a novel Lagrangian motion magnification method for facial minute movements. Our innovation encompasses three aspects: initially, we adapt a deep learning framework by incorporating precise optical flow data derived from a facial dataset to enhance facial video optical flow analysis. This enables efficient and accurate facial video optical flow analysis. Secondly, given that micro-movements are localized both spatially and temporally, we recommend approximating the optical flow field by utilizing both spatial and temporal sparse components, resulting in a double sparse decomposition. Thirdly, we utilize this decomposition to enhance specific facial regions, where we introduce a forward warping technique that divides the image grid into triangles and interpolates RGB vectors using barycentric coordinates at the transformed triangles' corners. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through diverse examples.

Recent advances in high-pressure synthesis methods have enabled researchers to produce high-quality samples with high indium content on the (Pb,In)Te compound, which has been found to have significantly increased superconducting transition temperatures compared to their lead-rich counterparts. This research investigates the London penetration depth, denoted by $\Delta \lambda(T)$, as a function of temperature in the compound In$_{0.8}$Pb$_{0.2}$Te. This compound is noted for its bulk $T_{c,onset}$ value of approximately 4.75 K and displays characteristics consistent with fully gapped BCS-like superconductivity, thereby ruling out the presence of topologically nontrivial A$_{2u}$ pairing; nonetheless, other pairing possibilities remain open, including odd-parity $A_{1u}$ pairing.

Human-AI co-creativity requires a partnership between humans and AI in creating a joint creative output, relying heavily on collaboration dynamics like turn-taking, communication, and contribution type. The interaction model is essential for a co-creative system's success. Unfortunately, interaction design is largely underrepresented in existing co-creative research and systems, which have predominantly focused on AI capabilities. This study emphasizes the significance of interaction design in co-creative systems, presenting the Co-Creative Framework for Interaction (COFI) to describe and analyze possible interaction models. COFI serves as a framework for researchers to study and categorize interaction models in existing co-creative systems, allowing them to identify areas for improvement. Through a dataset analysis of 92 existing co-creative systems, COFI offers a basis for categorizing interaction models, providing insights to shift focus towards more collaborative human-AI partnerships.

We integrate the concepts of mixed-space quantum representations in the areas of Condensed Matter Physics and Quantum Field Theory into a unified framework. This unifying approach hinges on the ability to expand quantum operators, encompassing bosons, fermions, and spin systems, using a universal basis operator involving mixed Hilbert spaces for momentum and position operators. These can be mapped onto creation and annihilation operators, where momentum is equivalent to the conjugate of a creation operator, and position is equivalent to a creation operator itself. The expansion coefficients derive from the Fourier transform of the Wigner quantum distribution function, known as the lattice Weyl transform. Consequently, various transformations such as fermionization via the Jordan-Wigner method and Holstein-Primakoff transformation from bosons to spin operators become accessible. Additionally, unitary transformations on creation and annihilation operators, as seen in the Bogoliubov transformation, can be applied, along with the Jordan-Schwinger transformation for matrix expressions, to streamline computational processes. Notably, our unification encompasses the well-established formulation of coherent states as a special case. Moreover, a new framework for Quantum Field Theory grounded in the Q-distribution of functional-field variables is proposed, along with a discussion on nonequilibrium quantum transport phenomena involving non-Hermitian operators and broken time-reversal symmetry in the appendix.

We analyze the weighted Lp affine surface areas, which have recently been featured in the Lp Steiner formula within the Lp Brunn Minkowski framework. The results demonstrate that these areas act as valuations on convex shapes, accompanied by isoperimetric inequalities. Moreover, the investigation reveals their connection to specific divergence metrics – the Kullback-Leibler and R\'enyi divergences – which compare the cone measures of a given shape and its polar.

Manganese-based nitride compounds with antiperovskite structures, including Mn$_3$NiN, exhibit complex magnetic behavior due to their kagome lattice. The resulting frustrated magnetic interactions, influenced by symmetric and asymmetric magnetic connections, can only be resolved in noncollinear configurations. Consequently, electronic interactions, which can be manipulated by external pressures such as epitaxial strain, significantly influence the properties of these systems. Therefore, the present work aimed to investigate how epitaxial strain imposed within the (111) plane affects the properties of such materials, while keeping magnetic and crystallographic symmetry unchanged. The findings revealed that the applied strain caused linear shifts in the band structure and the availability of states near the Fermi level. Notably, compressive strain reduced Mn-Mn distances within the kagome plane but linearly increased the distance between stacked kagome lattices, thus altering the availability of states near the Fermi level. Despite the linear variation of the availability of states across the Fermi energy, the anomalous Hall conductivity demonstrated a non-linear behavior. The $\sigma_{111}$ conductivity was significantly reduced under tensile strain and experienced a 26% increase with a 1.5% compression. The observed behavior was attributed to the non-divergent Berry curvature in the kagome plane, which increased under constraining forces but decreased under expansive strain.

Unlocking the full potential of upcoming large-scale universe surveys requires extracting non-standard insights from complex structure formation patterns. Despite their significance, these insights remain difficult to analyze due to the intricate theories and calculations involved. To overcome this challenge, researchers propose a set of statistical tools, based on wavelet transformations, to efficiently process and interpret data. These wavelet-based statistics leverage spatial averages and can capture a wide range of information from 3D data sets. Utilizing various types of 3D wavelets and employing advanced statistical modeling techniques, researchers demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach in analyzing matter field data. According to simulations, these statistics yielded superior accuracy, significantly improving the precision of parameter constraints for fundamental cosmological models and even the combined mass of neutrinos, as compared to traditional methods based on power spectrum analysis.

We derive limit theorems for the frequency of a specific pattern at the fringe 
of a randomly selected ranked tree-child network, expanding upon a limit law 
for cherries discovered by Bienvenu et al. in 2022. We find that for fringe 
patterns with heights of 1 or 2, their occurrences are predominantly either very 
common (mean occurrence rate increases linearly and follows a normal distribution) 
or relatively rare (mean occurrence rate remains constant and is governed by a 
Poisson distribution) or non-existent (mean occurrence rate approaches zero and 
has a degenerate distribution). We speculate that these three possibilities represent 
the sole potential outcomes for the frequency of any fringe pattern.

A recent law has sparked interest in machine unlearning, a concept where certain training samples are removed from predictive models as if they never existed. This process may also be triggered by faulty or adversarial data or a user's evolving desire for increased privacy. Models that don't require retraining can unlearn by simply deleting their closest related data, but this strategy is impractical for models with complex understanding. New optimization techniques can unlearn effectively but are hindered by their large computational demands due to the complex mathematical inverses involved. We utilize a novel metric, a variant of L-CODEC, which identifies model parameters most relevant to individual samples and can unlearn effectively without inverting large matrices. This makes it suitable not just for machine unlearning, but also for deep unlearning, vision applications and potentially other tasks such as face recognition and natural language processing. A GitHub repository containing the LCODEC code can be found at https://github.com/vsingh-group/LCODEC-deep-unlearning/

There's a significant gap in the research regarding machine learning (ML) requirements engineering, resulting in various issues and challenges during system specification, design, and development. To improve the reliability of ML-enabled systems, it's essential to place greater emphasis on requirements engineering for ML. Building upon insights gathered from past studies and industry experiences, this work presents a catalogue of 45 concerns that requirements engineers should consider when developing ML-enabled systems. This catalogue encompasses five key perspectives: objectives, user experience, infrastructure, model, and data, addressing concerns like the execution engine and telemetry for infrastructure, as well as explainability and reproducibility for models. A focus group involving eight software professionals validated the catalogue's importance, quality, and usability, leading to refinements and affirming its practical utility. The research's primary contribution is offering a validated, structured set of concerns that can guide requirements engineers in defining ML-enabled systems.

The significance of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy is investigated within the frameworks of AdS/CFT and finite-dimensional holographic quantum error correction. Specifically, within the realm of operator algebra quantum error correction, we introduce a generalization of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy over finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras, thereby establishing key equivalencies. This generalization shows that the bulk and boundary relative Renyi entropies are equal if and only if specific conditions related to encoding, the Ryu-Takayanagi formula, and subregion duality are met. This extends an existing equivalence theorem previously established in arxiv:1607.03901. Subsequently, the discussion focuses on a modular operator definition of sandwiched Renyi relative entropy and its suitability for finite-dimensional holographic quantum error correction. Lastly, the calculation of sandwiched Renyi relative entropies for a simple holographic random tensor network model is explored to understand the impact of corrections on the bulk and boundary relative Renyi entropy equality.

The influence of low-excitation radio galaxies on the life cycles of large galaxies is significant in our local universe. Nonetheless, research on these galaxies' evolution and the effect of their active cores on early galactic development is still lacking in understanding. Using the initial release of data from the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey, a team analyzed a dataset of 10481 low-excitation radio galaxies to investigate the evolution of their radio luminosity function up to a redshift of 2.5. The results indicate that this evolution is moderate. The researchers further categorized the galaxies into quiescent and star-forming galaxies and found that a substantial new population of low-excitation radio galaxies resides in star-forming galaxies at higher redshifts. The occurrence of these galaxies in quiescent galaxies displays a strong relationship with the galaxies' stellar mass up to a redshift of 1.5, similar to findings on accretion caused by the cooling of gas in galaxy haloes. The low-excitation radio galaxies hosted by quiescent galaxies are the dominant population at redshifts less than one and decrease with increasing redshift while showing an increase in characteristic luminosity. The low-excitation radio galaxies hosted by star-forming galaxies display an opposite pattern by increasing with redshift and eventually surpassing their counterparts in terms of space density. The occurrence of these galaxies in star-forming galaxies shows little correlation with the galaxies' stellar mass and also tends to increase with redshift, suggesting a different fueling mechanism related to the cold gas present in star-forming galaxies.

This paper develops new concepts of annular settling and output annular settling for nonlinear systems, and it formulates the criteria for short-term stability, boundedness, and settling in generalized Persidskii systems driven by bounded inputs, all based on verifying linear matrix inequalities. An example application in recurrent neural networks demonstrates the value of these new notions and conditions.

Determining the precise displacement of a mechanical oscillator or a microwave field along a specific direction within phase space is achievable by using trapped ions or superconducting circuits, coupled with ancilla qubits that transfer and then read out the displacement information. Nevertheless, accurately determining displacement in an arbitrary direction within phase space has not been feasible in such oscillator-qubit systems. We suggest implementing a hybrid setup combining an oscillator and qubits through feasible Rabi interactions for the precise estimation of phase space displacements in any direction. Utilizing this Rabi interferometer-based hybrid setup, our study demonstrates that it significantly outperforms single-mode schemes and traditional interferometers using Jaynes-Cummings interactions for quantum sensing. Notably, this Rabi interferometer shows sensitivity that remains unchanged regardless of the oscillator's thermal occupation level, hence there's no need for pre-cooling it to the ground state. We also examined the effects of qubit dephasing and oscillator thermalization, and despite their impact, our findings show that this interferometer retains its performance capabilities, even when dephasing and thermalization are at a considerable level and surpassing other comparative estimation schemes.

Designers encounter significant challenges in optimizing designs that must satisfy multiple goals, a process complicated further by expensive and extensive evaluations in Human-Computer Interaction. To assist designers, computational models can generate design examples, but they rely on a predefined model of the interaction domain, whereas alternative 'black box' methods can tackle any design issue. Nonetheless, research has been conducted primarily by experts or users, leaving a knowledge gap on the effectiveness of these methods for actual designers. This paper investigates the use of Bayesian optimization as an algorithmic tool to facilitate the design optimization process. By recommending the next design candidate to a designer based on prior observations, the algorithm helps designers explore a broader design space and achieve better solutions. Nonetheless, designers utilizing this method reported decreased autonomy and self-expression, even though they exhibited lower mental effort and less stress. In conclusion, human-in-the-loop optimization may benefit novice designers where personal involvement is less crucial.

To examine graded Frobenius algebras from a ring-theoretic viewpoint, we first establish definitions for graded quasi-Frobenius rings, graded Frobenius rings, and their shifted variants, and then explore their properties and representations. Furthermore, we revisit and expand upon existing theories of graded simple left Artinian rings, graded semisimple rings, as well as grade the Jacobson radical, singular radical, and their association with finiteness and injectivity criteria. Moreover, we prove a structural characterization for both regular and shifted versions of graded Frobenius rings.

This thesis offers novel optimization methods to tackle various issues within quantum information theory. Firstly, an algorithm for accurately estimating quantum states is presented. This algorithm relies on orthogonal projections across intersecting planes determined by the associated probability distributions and measurement operators, showcasing its performance in both speed and accuracy in the presence of realistic errors. Furthermore, we present a method for quantifying quantum non-locality by identifying the optimal Bell inequality given a set of bipartite measurement frequencies. Lastly, to investigate the quantum marginal problem, an operator and corresponding algorithm have been developed to determine if a given set of quantum marginals and eigenvalues can be reconciled with a compatible density matrix.

We examine a flat FLRW model within the framework of f(R,T)-gravity, incorporating a quadratic R-curvature variation and a linear T-term. Our results indicate that the model behaves like a late universe characterized by accelerating expansion, ultimately resulting in a big rip. A parametrized scale factor a(t) model is proposed, initially starting as a point singularity with zero volume, infinite energy density, and infinite temperature. The model features accelerated expansion at present and mimics the behavior of the Lambda-CDM model at late times. Furthermore, our proposed model is consistent with the quintessence dark energy model at present and aligns with the standard Lambda-CDM cosmology at late times.

We investigate the correlations between fields associated with a pair of entangled quarks in the context of the super Yang-Mills theory, utilizing holographic methods to analyze the dynamics. Our analysis considers a string in AdS space that represents these entangled quarks, with endpoints either static or moving at constant acceleration. We derive the two-point correlators of the fields describing the linearized perturbations on the string worldsheet, thereby obtaining the long-time behavior of the correlations. Notably, in the accelerated case, the string worldsheet geometry exhibits the properties of a two-sided AdS black hole with a wormhole, embodying the ER=EPR conjecture. Our findings indicate that causality fundamentally influences the nature of the particle dispersion relation and the features of the induced interaction between two particles from the field. Specifically, in the disconnected case, each particle exhibits dissipative dynamics regardless of distance, with the interaction vanishing in the long term according to a power law, whereas, in the connected case, the induced dispersion relation becomes non-dissipative at long times. We will further explore the implications of our results for the dynamics of entangled particles and the ER=EPR conjecture.

A cosmological model in $f(R)$-gravity has been explored, characterized by a cubic equation in scalar curvature $R$.  We've accounted for the energy resulting from nonlinear $f(R)$ curvature inspired geometry, discovering an accelerating universe expansion with an anti-gravitating negative pressure. Key parameters were numerically solved and validated using 86 Hubble observations across a broad redshift range. Our examination of model evolution using observational data revealed an accelerating universe transition occurring at $z_{tr} \simeq 0.694069$, in line with the predictions of $\Lambda$CDM. Furthermore, state finder analysis confirms the consistency of our model with $\Lambda$CDM in late universe epochs, based on detailed plots of model dynamical parameters.

Recent machine learning techniques have found widespread use in diagnosing machinery faults. However, the main disadvantage of these methods is their inability to provide transparent explanations due to their 'black box' nature. This paper introduces a groundbreaking neural network structure known as the temporal logic neural network (TLNN). The unique feature of TLNN is that its neurons are defined by logical statements, allowing the network to be expressed and analyzed using a weighted signal temporal logic. Unlike traditional neural networks, TLNN retains their benefits while offering a clear, formally expressed understanding of its internal workings. Experimental results with actual datasets demonstrate that the proposed network delivers highly accurate and efficient fault diagnosis. Furthermore, the integration of formal language into the network enables the provision of insight into the decision-making process, resulting in interpretable fault diagnosis.

When cooling a complex quantum system from a hot, unstable state to a precise point of phase transition, we examine how well it stays in a stable state, meaning, we study how well it stays in the same state over time. Our study reveals that there are certain general patterns that govern how well this works in this process, patterns that depend on certain key characteristics of the system itself and its transition to a new phase. These patterns apply to various cooling processes regardless of specific circumstances, showing how we can understand key properties of a system in a precise moment by looking at it at any moment during its transition to that moment, rather than only after it has completed the transition.

We show that a simple, analog transmission approach in conjunction with match filtering can effectively emulate the role of an edge server within a federated learning framework, allowing for large-scale, edge-serverless implementation of the technology even when numerous users are involved. Furthermore, we have developed a specialized training algorithm that enables user equipment to engage in uninterrupted local computations, thus fully capitalizing on their processing capabilities. The proposed methods' efficiency has been quantified through convergence rate derivations, with results indicating that when interference is Gaussian-distributed, these algorithms exhibit convergence rates similar to those achieved in server-based FL settings. Conversely, heavy-tailed interference distributions result in reduced convergence speeds that worsen with increasing tail heftiness. Our findings reveal that parallel computation of both data and communication significantly shortens overall system runtime, with the greatest benefits realized in scenarios characterized by substantial communication latency. The efficacy of these approaches is substantiated through comprehensive simulation testing.

This study delves into higher-order generalized moment functions, drawing parallels with the binomial type functions, which have been explored in abstract frameworks. Our preceding work investigated the properties of generalized moment functions of higher order on commutative groups. In this present work, we expand our research into a more abstract setting, focusing on hypergroups. We establish a characterization of generalized moment functions on the one-variable polynomial hypergroup, using the partial derivatives of an analytic function and polynomial composition. Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula for the moment generating functions of rank at most two on the Tchebyshev hypergroup as an example.

Our GraphMoE approach employs a neural network that generates random graphs by learning the distribution of these graphs, where a moment estimator helps guide the training process. We leverage graphlets as training features, subgraph counts that provide information about the local structure of small-sized graph subunits. The neural network takes random noise as input and generates node vector representations, allowing the realisation of graphs that can accurately imitate datasets in various domains such as chemistry, medicine and social networks. These artificially generated graphs exhibit sufficient similarity to target data to convincingly deceive discriminator neural networks, capable of differentiating between diverse types of random graphs.

Multi-purpose models excel at specific tasks, but their limitations become apparent when real-world applications necessitate handling multiple tasks and adjusting to different domains. Recent advancements in instructional prompts have improved their ability to generalize across tasks, but their combined effect with Multi-Task Learning (MTL) has not been extensively studied in the biomedical field. To address this, the authors of this paper investigate the influence of instructional prompts on biomedical MTL. They created BoX, a collection of 32 tasks in biomedical Natural Language Processing, and introduced In-BoXBART, a unified model capable of learning all tasks within BoX without task-specific components. To date, this is the first attempt to develop a unified model in the biomedical field using instructional prompts for task generalization. Experimental findings show that the proposed model outperforms both the single-task and multi-task (without instructional prompts) baselines and demonstrates improved performance in few-shot learning.

We identify the limiting distribution for a family of values, expressed as a function of the fundamental discriminant $D$, where $\epsilon$ falls within a specified range and $\chi_D$ represents the corresponding real character associated with $D$. This investigation also provides an upper bound for the rate of convergence towards its limiting distribution. The obtained result further enables the derivation of an asymptotic bound for small absolute values of the function in question, involving the ratio $L'/L$ at a particular point.

Recent research in hyperspectral unmixing has increasingly utilized deep learning techniques, specifically with autoencoder architecture, to enhance the effectiveness of unmixing. To optimize the performance of the unmixing network, we suggest a unique architecture with a pseudo-ground truth for abundances and an approximation network to enhance spatial correlations. In the proposed Guided Encoder-Decoder Architecture for Hyperspectral Unmixing with Spatial Smoothness, we utilize one-hot encoded abundances and exclude prior hyperspectral unmixing methods by using k-means to compute abundances. To release the single-layer constraint, we integrate the unmixing network's outputs into the mixing network, different from traditional hyperspectral unmixing with autoencoder. In further modifications, we experimented with concatenating the unmixing and mixing networks in the GAUSS blind method and utilizing abundance results from a signal processing method as pseudo-ground truth in the GAUSS prime method. Results on four experimental datasets indicate that these architectures either outperformed or matched the performance of existing hyperspectral unmixing algorithms from both deep learning and signal processing domains.

In a 4D spacetime framework utilizing Celestial variables, we analyze 2-2 scattering using a crossing-symmetric dispersion relation to re-express Celestial amplitudes in terms of crossing-symmetric partial waves that exhibit singularities. By applying locality constraints in local theories, we derive analytical expressions that lead to new bounds on partial wave moments, enabling us to quantify the degree of scalar dominance. Additionally, we explore a unique positivity that appears across a wide range of theories, revealing that this positivity only occurs in theories where spin-0 is dominant. By removing spurious singularities from crossing-symmetric partial waves, we uncover the remarkable properties of 'Feynman blocks' in the Celestial variable, which include typically realness. This realness is further utilized through Geometric Function Theory techniques to derive non-projective bounds on Wilson coefficients in terms of partial wave moments.

To efficiently compress large-scale pre-trained language models, researchers have explored methods like Contrastive Learning, Intermediate Layer Distillation, Data Augmentation, and Adversarial Training. A novel data augmentation approach tailored for knowledge distillation is proposed, dubbed CILDA. By utilizing intermediate layer representations of the primary task and a contrastive loss to refine masked adversarial data augmentation, CILDA stands out as the first to do so. This learning-based augmentation technique significantly outperforms existing KD frameworks in both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations.

Cuesta-Conway numbers, also known as surreal numbers, provide an extended mathematical framework by incorporating elements of real and ordinal values. Their straightforward definition involves their normal forms as indexed exponentials of ordinals. This extension naturally facilitates addition, multiplication, and a total order, effectively forming an ordered system. By systematically building this framework, we derive a sequence of real-closed fields that lay foundational groundwork, culminating in a demonstration of the surreal numbers as a totally ordered, commutative, real-closed field.

Tasks such as unsupervised text style transfer have seen an increase in the application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) due to controlled text generation. However, incorporating RL into such tasks poses a significant challenge as sparse rewards are only available after text generation is complete, making it sample-inefficient and hard to converge, particularly due to the large action space involved. Existing strategies, including reward-shaping methods, have shown little improvement in this area. In contrast, our proposed approach involves providing a dense reward for each token generated during the text generation process. We evaluate our method's effectiveness through unsupervised text style transfer, where we find that our system significantly improves over existing systems by 21% in terms of human evaluation and 12% in terms of automated evaluation, on average across various datasets. Additionally, our method outperforms the current best reward-shaping approach ('roll-out strategy') by 22% in terms of style transfer quality, as assessed by human evaluation, while reducing training samples by 2.5 times and cutting down training time by 7 times.
This article aims to provide a conclusive proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The particle in a box is a straightforward model with a classical Hamiltonian defined by the equation $H=p^2$, utilizing $2m=1$, and confined within a specific spatial region, $-b<q<b$, where $0<b<\infty$. Thanks to its simplicity, this model has been extensively analyzed using canonical quantization and serves as a typical introduction for students to comprehend the fundamental concepts. However, recent examination has revealed an inconsistency in previous conclusions. The procedures involved in affine quantization not only highlight the quantization problem but also yield a valid quantization approach, which necessarily results in more complex eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, requiring further investigation.

Recent benchmarks in machine learning have indicated that advancements in
specific sub-fields may have been overstated, as several studies have failed to
achieve progress in accordance with reported literature. Irreproducibility of
results from model comparison studies is partly to blame, which often neglect
key sources of unreliability, making results unverifiable to external parties.
Our primary aim is to examine and summarize the literature on irreproducibility
issues in machine learning studies, presenting a structured classification
framework and discussing its key contributors, before suggesting potential areas
for further research, specifically three key directions for exploration.

Deep learning in scientific contexts is highly effective at establishing connections in data, but its widespread adoption has been hindered by difficulties in understanding these learned associations. The Information Bottleneck framework is an essential tool for grasping relationships between input and output by considering a balance between the precision and simplicity of approximations to these connections. We demonstrate a critical enhancement of the Information Bottleneck approach that greatly expands its capabilities as a method of deep learning analysis in scientific contexts. The Distributed Information Bottleneck framework limits the complexity of the relationships between different components of the input, breaking down the relationships identified by deep learning into meaningful approximations that do not require tailored datasets or network architectures. When applied to intricate systems, this technique sheds new light on the systems by tightly controlling and tracking the amount of information drawn from various components in each approximation. The Distributed IB's explanatory value has been illustrated through its application in both theoretical and experimental physics, such as in deconstructing Boolean circuits into informative input components and analyzing the structural basis for plastic deformation in materials. Ultimately, the Distributed IB's structured scheme for making approximations greatly improves the interpretability of deep learning models, thus empowering the examination of complex systems at an unprecedented level.

To determine how well NLP models can handle unseen tasks with given guidelines, we've developed Super-NaturalInstructions, a vast collection of 1,616 unique tasks with expert-created guidelines, encompassing 76 diverse task categories. This dataset allows us to comprehensively evaluate cross-task generalization, specifically how well a model trained on one set of tasks can apply instructions to an unrelated set. We also designed Tk-Instruct, a transformer-based model that can interpret various in-context instructions. Experimental results show Tk-Instruct significantly outperforms previous instruction-following models by over 9%, while using a significantly smaller model size. We analyzed the effect of different factors, such as task exposure, instance quantity, and model size on generalization, aiming to contribute to advancements in creating versatile NLP models.

Research into new $4d/5d$ transition metal systems, particularly iridate materials and $\alpha$-RuCl$_{3}$, has garnered significant attention due to their $J_{\text{eff}}=\frac{1}{2}$ state and Kitaev interactions. In our study, we successfully create a $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$ state with Ising interactions by modulating the balance between spin-orbit interaction and trigonal crystal field splitting in Li$_{2}$RhO$_{3}$ through a topochemical transformation into Ag$_{3}$LiRh$_{2}$O$_{6}$. This process yields increased trigonal distortion and reduced spin-orbit coupling, which allows for a new expression of the $\mu=\frac{1}{2}$ state using perturbation theory. The result is a notable difference in the ground state and corresponding magnetic behavior, transitioning from a 6 K spin-glass in Li$_{2}$RhO$_{3}$ to a 94 K antiferromagnet in Ag$_{3}$LiRh$_{2}$O$_{6}$. This groundbreaking finding provides an avenue to explore a wide range of magnetic states and create a diverse magnetic phase diagram.

Developing effective and stable solvers for time-dependent partial differential equations presents a major challenge. To address this issue, we propose using graph neural networks as a means of learning computationally efficient solutions via message-passing models. Firstly, we derive a representation of PDE data that accounts for physical phenomena using domain invariant features. Subsequently, we apply graph structures to unstructured meshes, demonstrating the potential of message-passing graph neural networks (MPGNNs) in parameterizing governing equations and learning solver schemes for linear and nonlinear PDEs. Moreover, we show that these solvers can operate independently of their initial geometric parameters, enabling solution finding across diverse complex domains. Furthermore, we apply a recurrent graph neural network approach to identify the sequential solutions of PDEs over time.

Single photon emitters are often detected using a Hanbury Brown and Twiss intensity interferometer consisting of a beamsplitter and two time-correlated counters. The autocorrelation function, which measures the coincidence of photon arrivals between the two detectors, typically displays a characteristic dip to zero when time equals zero for a genuine SPE. Conventionally, SPEs are identified based on a criterion where the autocorrelation function at zero time is less than half the expected value. This work employs stochastic methods to simulate the effect of non-perfect detection equipment and optics on identifying SPEs. The simulation demonstrates that detecting SPEs becomes unreliable when detectors are inefficiently matched and detector noise significantly exceeds half the SPE's actual emission rate.

Our CSPI camera, employing complementary detection and optimized Bernoulli modulation, effectively mitigates interference from ambient light in single-pixel imaging, allowing it to operate optimally even in high-disturbance conditions. Simulations show that the CSPI camera maintains disturbance-free operation when the coded pattern is set to P=0.5, outperforming SPI under varying disturbance intensities. Reconstruction comparisons with SPI and differential SPI reveal the CSPI camera's superiority, ultimately facilitating the practical application of single-pixel Lidar technology.

This work investigates a range of finite element methods to address a more complex set of interface problems. We specifically focus on one-dimensional elliptic problems with discontinuous solutions and interface jump conditions that are either implicit or of the Robin type. A significant challenge in developing generalized finite element methods lies in creating suitable enrichment functions that account for the imposed solution discontinuity while controlling the increase of the condition number. A recently developed stable generalized finite element method was initially constructed using a single enrichment function, which we have now generalized using multiple simple one-sided discontinuous enrichment functions of varying degrees. We have successfully established optimal order convergence in both the $L^2$ and $H^1$-norms, as well as optimal order convergence at all nodes. The effectiveness of this stable generalized finite element method has been demonstrated through its application to a multi-layer wall model of drug-eluting stents, which incorporates zero-flux jump conditions and implicit concentration interface conditions.

The stabilizer states of $n$ qubits are those states that remain unchanged under a group of transformations with $2^n$ elements derived from the Pauli group. The set of Clifford gates generates unitary transformations that preserve these states. We identify a physically motivated subset of Clifford gates - Hadamard, phase, and CNOT gates - that induce a graph structure, known as "reachability graphs," on the set of stabilizers. We explicitly construct these reachability graphs for systems of $n\le 5$ qubits. When we limit the set of Clifford gates used, the reachability graphs decompose into several connected components with complex relationships. We examine a restricted version of these graphs built from Hadamard and CNOT gates operating on two qubits. We show how these simple subgraphs evolve into more intricate ones at three and four qubits. We argue that beyond four qubits, no additional subgraph structures emerge. Instead, we observe that the entropic structures inside the subgraphs become increasingly complex with growing qubit numbers. Specifically, we observe that certain stabilizer states at four qubits have non-allowed entropic vectors based on holographic entropy principles. We reflect on the characteristics of the transition between holographic and non-holographic states as observed in the stabilizer reachability graphs.

The MultiEarth 2022 competition represents the inaugural event focused on
forest surveillance and deforestation analysis within the Amazon rainforest
regardless of weather and time. Its primary objective is to standardize a common
benchmark for integrating multiple information types and unite researchers from
earth and environmental sciences with those specializing in multimodal learning
to comparatively assess diverse approaches to predicting deforestation under
unified and strictly comparable circumstances. Comprising three components,
MultiEarth 2022 will include sub-challenges centered around matrix filling, 
forest area estimation, and visual image transformation. This article provides
detailed instructions for participating in the challenge, alongside the relevant
datasets and evaluation criteria. Additional information can be accessed at
https://sites.google.com/view/rainforest-challenge.

Recent studies have highlighted the significance of reconciling conflicting goals in model development, including accuracy versus fairness, or disparate measures of fairness. This balancing act falls under a broader category of multi-objective optimization problems, where optimization techniques strive to find Pareto optimal compromises between competing objectives. Our work initiates with a novel, differentiable metric that permits direct optimization of fairness across different groups during model training, particularly, achieving balance in accuracy across diverse groups. Subsequently, we propose two versatile model-agnostic frameworks for learning Pareto optimal parameterizations across different subsets of neural classification models. Our approaches are tested in the domain of hate speech identification, a domain in which earlier studies have documented a lack of fairness across speakers of various English dialects. Our experiments, conducted across convolutional, sequential, and transformer-based neural architectures, reveal superior trade-offs between accuracy and fairness compared to existing research. Crucially, our measure allows the Pareto optimization process to guarantee that each architecture achieves the optimal trade-off between fairness and accuracy relative to the dataset, subject to user-defined tolerance for errors.

The technique of intercalation allows researchers to modify the electronic properties of graphene and create stable, two-dimensional layers of elements with distinct characteristics by exploiting quantum confinement. Our study focuses on a monolayer of graphene on a SiC substrate, where lead atoms have been inserted between the graphene and SiC, yielding a neutral state with an exceptionally high p-type charge carrier density. Our findings, obtained through advanced microscopy techniques and low-energy electron diffraction, reveal that the inserted lead atoms contribute additional bands in the low-energy electronic structure, forming a moiré superlattice that cannot be predicted from existing models. These experiments illustrate how intercalation can be used to achieve 2D confinement and potentially lead to superconductivity at the graphene/SiC interface.

Conversational AI systems typically evaluate potential responses based on the similarity between their representations and the current dialogue context. Yet, their effectiveness is limited when trained using a single context, as real conversations often deviate from scripted scenarios. This paper introduces an innovative framework that incorporates multiple variations of a dialogue context to enhance learning. By combining contrastive learning as a secondary goal, the model can generate robust representations that remain consistent even with perturbations made during testing. The proposed approach integrates well with current augmentation methods and significantly outperforms standard BERT-based models. Furthermore, we introduce ConMix, a novel data augmentation method that introduces random mixing of context tokens, demonstrating its superior performance and capacity to generate more resilient dialogue representations.

Imitation learning for teaching robots complex manipulation skills can be done efficiently without needing precise rewards or extensive computing power. Nevertheless, imitation learning methods are hampered by the need for advanced data collection systems and have difficulty generalizing beyond the training data. One way to overcome this limitation is by gathering more data representing real-world operating conditions. This work focuses on characteristics of such additional demonstration data and their effects on performance. We analyze the effects of demonstrations with intentional corrections and randomly sampled demonstrations on a robot hand's ability to complete a pick-and-place task using its five fingers. Our results show that corrective demonstrations outperform randomly sampled demonstrations when there are many additional demonstrations covering various scenarios, whereas the type of demonstrations does not matter when there are ample original demonstrations. Our research reveals a trade-off between collecting corrections and their usefulness. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of inexpensive sensors, such as the LeapMotion, in lowering the costs of data collection for complex manipulation tasks. Our project is open-sourced at https://github.com/GT-STAR-Lab/corrective-demos-dexterous-manipulation.

This paper outlines the BLCU-ICALL system that successfully participated in the Definition Modeling subtrack of the SemEval-2022 Task 1, achieving superior results in multiple languages. To tackle this challenge, we developed a transformer-based multitasking framework that combines multiple embedding architectures through cross-attention and captures gloss structure with a masking language model objective. Furthermore, our study examines an efficient model ensembling strategy to enhance robustness. The evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of our solution. The accompanying code can be accessed via https://github.com/blcuicall/SemEval2022-Task1-DM.

Understanding the life cycles of stars and the structure of our galaxy is made easier by studying open clusters.
