Evaluation results on VisDial v1.0 and v0.9 datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves the current best performance on both datasets. Furthermore, we observe substantial improvements when working with limited data (up to 9.35 point gain on NDCG metric).

To combat errors in difficult-to-access qubits, highly sensitive spectator qubits (SQs) are utilized to detect noise, providing infrequent, yet crucial corrections to the data qubits. A novel, Bayesian approach leveraging complex mapping effectively optimizes adaptive measurement strategies and correction protocols. For instances such as decoherence induced by random noise, this approach results in significantly reduced errors. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness scales exponentially with the SQ's sensitivity, demonstrating the potential for robust qubit stabilization within specified conditions.

Text generation inconsistencies often plague AI systems, with real-world applications heavily relying on the accuracy of the text produced by Data-to-Text (D2T) systems. To tackle this challenge, we present R2D2, a comprehensive training framework for D2T that equips a model with two primary roles - generating text and assessing its credibility - along with two supplementary tasks to enhance its ability to identify inaccuracies and recognize untrustworthy content. To support R2D2's training process, we develop a couple of methods to generate unreliable text samples. Furthermore, we emphasize that a significant shortcoming of D2T systems is their weakness in identifying specific entities, which significantly contributes to the inaccuracy issue. Consequently, we recommend the incorporation of Natural Language Processing (NLP) metrics based on named entity recognition into the evaluation framework for D2T text output. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the R2D2 system in minimizing text inaccuracies, with remarkable achievements on the FeTaQA, LogicNLG, and ToTTo benchmark datasets.

The primary objective of this thesis is to investigate potential attack pathways targeting the Iota network's 2.0 protocol and conduct a comprehensive analysis of their feasibility. In this work, we examine existing attack strategies in Distributed Ledger Technologies, evaluate their applicability to the Iota 2.0 protocol, and specifically identify a targeted attack on an honest participant's ability to write to the ledger within a network comprising full nodes operating on a particular software version.

The development of effective massively multilingual image captioning systems has been hindered by a shortage of reliable evaluation datasets. To address this challenge, we introduce the Crossmodal-3600 dataset (XM3600), which comprises a diverse collection of 3600 images from around the world, accompanied by human-translated captions in 36 languages. These captions exhibit uniform style across languages and were crafted to circumvent the pitfalls of direct translation. Our evaluation demonstrates that utilizing the XM3600 dataset as a standard for assessing automatic metrics leads to improved correlation with human ratings in massively multilingual image captioning model selection.

We present FLEURS, a benchmark designed to evaluate the universality of speech representations through few-shot learning in 102 languages. Constructed upon the machine translation FLoRes-101 dataset, this n-way parallel speech benchmark encompasses roughly 12 hours of speech supervision per language. The FLEURS dataset is applicable to various speech tasks such as Automatic Speech Recognition, Speech Language Identification, Translation, and Retrieval. Our study offers baseline performances using multilingual pre-trained models, like mSLAM, with the primary aim of advancing speech technology in underrepresented languages and driving research in low-resource speech comprehension.

Event extraction's progress is hindered by data scarcity and imbalance. To address this challenge, we introduce the self-training with gradient guidance (STGG) framework, which comprises two components. First, a base event extraction model is initially trained using existing annotations, then it is applied to large datasets lacking annotations to predict newly discovered event triggers and their associated arguments. Next, a scoring model evaluates each predicted event's likelihood by analyzing its path within an Abstract Meaning Representation graph. This analysis generates scores indicating the correctness of these predictions. These predictions and their associated correctness scores are then used to fine-tune the base model, leveraging the correctness scores as gradient guidance. Our experiments demonstrate that STGG enhances event extraction performance by up to 1.9 F-score on ACE05-E, ACE05-E+, and ERE-EN datasets. Furthermore, the analysis shows that STGG's general applicability allows it to be adapted to various base event extraction models and enhance their performance by tapping into broad unlabeled datasets even without high-quality graph annotations.

The cartoon domain has gained significant attention in recent times, yet, previous attempts to transform high-quality portrait images into cartoons have been met with challenges due to key constraints, including a high requirement for extensive training images and limited support for abstract cartoon faces. Recent advancements using the layer swapping technique for stylization with reduced training images still fall short due to remaining issues. This paper introduces a new method, referred to as Cross-domain Style mixing, which successfully combines and integrates different latent codes from separate domains. Our approach efficiently stylizes various cartoon faces with distinct levels of abstraction using a single generator, eliminating the need for large-scale training images.

Multilingual question-answering systems heavily rely on document retrieval and answer extraction from these retrieved documents to produce top answer candidates.
It is theorized that open-domain multilingual QA systems are highly susceptible to inconsistent information when dealing with texts in multiple languages due to these documents often providing a model with varying details about a single subject.
Our goal is to grasp the influence of information asymmetry and cultural factors by investigating how retrieval bias affects multilingual open-domain QA models. 
In our analysis, we will assess whether diverse retriever models return distinct passages in response to the same query in different languages on TyDi QA and XOR-TyDi QA, two datasets for multilingual QA, to determine the existence of retrieval disparities. 
Our speculation is that variations in content among texts across languages may indicate divergences in cultural contexts and social biases.

A novel, high-dimensional linear regression method is proposed that constructs asymptotically precise tests for subsets of regression coefficient hypotheses through resampling. It enables the integration of any multiple testing procedure for making confidence claims about relevant predictors. By utilizing permutation-based test statistics and combining repeated data splits with variable selection techniques, it creates individual hypothesis tests that are suitably aggregated to produce subset tests. This methodology is highly versatile as it accommodates various selection techniques and combining functions, and it can be presented in exact and approximate forms. We have designed it to handle larger dimensions more efficiently by reducing memory usage and computation time. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we provide simulation and gene expression analysis results using real data.

Current machine translation models still face difficulties when dealing with challenging inputs such as noisy data and subtle variations in language. Previous research has attempted to address this issue by focusing on specific types of noise, but there remains a lack of understanding about minor variations in language nuance that maintain the original meaning. We define and formalize this category of variation, called Natural Asymmetrical Variation, and investigate its impact on machine translation robustness. Our findings show that current models struggle with NAV, but can be improved with human-generated variations. Additionally, we find that NAV robustness can be applied across languages and that artificial perturbations can replicate some of the benefits, but not all, of real NAV data.

Standard mathematical approaches like discrete integration and gradient descent rely heavily on linear algebra and therefore are only suitable for use with state vectors in Euclidean spaces, as described in current literature. However, by modifying these methods and applying the concepts from the SO(3) and SE(3) Lie groups, rotations and rigid body motions can be effectively handled, providing a detailed analysis of various representations and their implications for calculations involving state vectors and motion analysis.

We examine the "eigenbundle" (localization bundle) associated with certain Hilbert modules over symmetric, bounded domains of rank $r$, yielding complex-analytic fibre spaces that have an $r+1$-stratification. The fibers are described from the perspective of K\"ahler geometry as line bundle sections over flag manifolds, and we derive the metric embedding by using derivatives of reproducing kernel functions. Notable instances include ideals defined by vanishing conditions on the distinct strata within the stratification.

We investigate a new technique for language models to generate text that adheres to predefined restrictions, while preserving fluency and performance on subsequent tasks. We present MuCoLa, a sampling strategy that combines the language model's likelihood with custom (differentiable) constraints within a unified scoring system, followed by non-autoregressive sampling. It starts with an entire sequence of random values, and then applies a Markov chain defined by Langevin Dynamics using gradients derived from the energy function. We test MuCoLa's effectiveness in generating text under soft and rigid constraints, as well as their combinations, and achieve notable improvements over comparable baselines in controlling toxicity, managing sentiment, and following keyword prompts.

Similar to other cybersecurity domains, machine learning has become a promising solution for detecting Android malware. Although numerous studies employing various algorithms and feature sets have demonstrated promising detection capabilities, a lack of reproducibility and standard evaluation protocols complicates the comparison of these approaches. This paper conducts an analysis of 10 prominent studies on Android malware detection using a unified evaluation framework. Through this comprehensive study, we identify five critical factors that, if overlooked during dataset creation and detector design, significantly influence the trained models' performance and accuracy. These factors include sample duplication, label attribution, class imbalance, evasion techniques, and evolving app characteristics. Our research reveals that existing ML-based detectors were evaluated under optimistic conditions, leading to their impressive reported results. Notably, our findings emphasize the importance of creating realistic experimental scenarios, considering these factors, to facilitate the development of more effective ML-based solutions for detecting Android malware.

Modern natural language processing (NLP) systems heavily rely on Large Language Models, delivering high accuracy across various tasks, but their computational demands pose significant challenges. Researchers have been investigating methods such as pruning, quantization, and distillation to mitigate the high cost and large size of these models. This study focuses on exploring how models pruned using a specific technique, Gradual Unstructured Magnitude Pruning, perform when transferred across different domains and tasks. Experimental results reveal that models pruned during the pretraining phase using a general masked language model can adapt effectively to new domains and tasks with minimal hyperparameter tuning. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that our sparse model, Sparse*BERT, can be transformed into SparseBioBERT by fine-tuning on biomedical text, achieving comparable quality to BioBERT while significantly reducing the number of parameters, to just 10%.

Cellular extensions at the forefront of a cell are critical in detecting signals from their surroundings, particularly during cell movement and expansion. New research indicates that these protrusions encircle surrounding fibers. Although the mechanisms behind this process are not well understood, we investigated the coiling of these cellular protrusions on fibers with different shapes using a combination of theoretical modeling and experiments. Our theoretical model explains how curved membrane proteins create cell protrusions that utilize the forces generated by actin polymerization, identifying the importance of membrane flexibility and adhesive forces in guiding the leading-edge of protrusions. This theoretical model predicted that round fibers promote coiling but that it halts on fibers with flat cross-sections. These predictions were validated through the use of high-resolution microscopy on suspended fibers, allowing for the capture of detailed images and measurements of coiling around fibers of varying diameters.

Deep learning model training on cardiac MRI faces difficulties due to the limited amount of expert-verified data and inherent data complexity. Recently, self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) has shown significant performance gains in several medical imaging areas, but the level of representation accuracy for the main organ of interest versus surrounding tissues remains uncertain. This work aims to explore incorporating anatomical prior knowledge into an SSCL framework. It involves using a heart localization network to segment the heart from MRI images and subsequent pretraining in multiple tasks using SSCL, revealing substantial improvements in downstream diagnostic capabilities through such method. Notably, pretraining with in-domain data generally yields better results, especially concerning saliency and performance when compared to end-to-end training and pretraining from general networks like ImageNet. Surprisingly, though, integrating anatomical prior knowledge doesn't seem to significantly enhance pretraining performance.

This research investigates the influence of Pauli-excluded nucleon-nucleon forces on the half-lives of heavy, even-even nuclei, specifically those with atomic numbers between 84 and 92. We adapted the Pauli exclusion principle to our analysis by re-evaluating nucleon-nucleon interactions based on the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization rule and incorporating a kinetic energy modification to the double-folding method. When we compared the calculated half-lives to the actual observed data, our approach showed an improvement when considering the energy transfer between alpha decay particles, with a reduced standard deviation from experimental results of 0.340 down to 0.309. It was found that accounting for kinetic energy using an extended Thomas-Fermi method more accurately aligned the calculated alpha decay lifetimes with measured data.

Research into the neutron-rich isotopes of Ca, Ni, Zr, and Sn using a continuum Skyrme Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov theory reveals promising exotic nuclear properties. The model successfully replicates experimentally determined two-neutron and one-neutron separation energies, resulting in significantly shorter drip lines when calculated using one-neutron energies. It was discovered that the neutron pairing energies in odd-numbered nuclei were significantly smaller compared to those in adjacent even-even nuclei due to the absence of pairing contributions from unpaired neutrons. Analysis of the single-particle structures, radii, and density distributions in these isotopes led to the prediction of halo structures in the neutron-rich Ca, Ni, and Sn isotopes. These halos feature large increases in radii and significant deviations from traditional scaling laws, along with very diffuse density distributions. It was determined that the primary contributors to these effects are orbitals located near the Fermi surface, particularly those with low angular momenta. Additionally, the numbers of neutrons in these orbitals and the behavior of pairing energies both suggest that the pairing correlations are critical factors in the development of halo phenomena.

The traditional DeGroot-style opinion formation model assumes ongoing interactions among social network members, but struggles with external entities that interact only briefly. Many real-world organizations and individuals fit this profile. As an example, a business may try to influence multiple consumers to buy their products, but can only do so within a specified time frame. We introduce an adapted DeGroot model, enabling temporary interactions between external and permanent agents, then investigate and model various strategies for an external entity to maximize its impact on opinion formation.

As the size and interconnectedness of networked control systems expand, the need to understand their ability to withstand failures becomes increasingly crucial. Recently, the application of graph theory in this field has gained momentum, sparking significant interest among researchers. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of using graph-theoretic methods to evaluate the robustness of networked control systems. It discusses various algorithms for distributed networks, explores how these systems resist intentional disruptions, and examines the structural properties of their underlying networks. The paper also presents mathematical techniques to assess the impact of malicious actions and offers a graph-based perspective on traditional notions of system robustness, thereby reducing the vulnerability of these systems to attacks. Furthermore, the discussion touches on various issues related to the security of networked control systems, with graph theory serving as a key analytical tool. Finally, the paper identifies several promising avenues for future research in this field.

The fundamental non-trivial vacuum states in QCD serve as the base of all matter, and we investigate this structure in detail through contemporary visualization methods. Specifically, our current research is concentrated on centre vortices found in the ground-state of lattice QCD. Notably, our focus has shifted towards understanding the influence of dynamical fermions in the QCD vacuum on centre-vortex structures, as these fermions have a substantial impact and significantly expand our knowledge of centre vortices' roles in the two fundamental aspects of QCD: confinement and chiral symmetry breaking.

When ions are densely packed, their mutual spatial restrictions significantly impact their interactions.  To address this issue, we explored the asymptotic behavior of the steady-state equations accounting for spatial restrictions.  We transformed the relevant equations into a Poisson-Boltzmann equation incorporating spatial effects, parameterized by $\Lambda$, and positive constants based on the size of the ions and solvent molecules.  The influence of these constants on the system was found to depend on a Lambert-type function representing the solvent concentration.  The model's asymptotic behavior as $\Lambda$ approaches infinity revealed a unique solution converging to that of a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation, thereby providing a generalized framework for such equations.

Recent advances in multi-agent reinforcement learning often rely on deep neural networks, but they are hard to understand for human experts. Existing work on interpretable reinforcement learning has been successful in creating decision tree-based policies from neural networks, but this has been achieved mainly in single-agent settings. To address this limitation, we developed the first set of algorithms that can extract interpretable decision tree-based policies from multi-agent reinforcement learning models. Our first algorithm, IVIPER, is a multi-agent extension of a recent method for single-agent interpretable reinforcement learning, and it yields high-quality decision tree-based policies for each agent. To further improve coordination between agents, we proposed a new algorithm, MAVIPER, which trains decision trees jointly by predicting the behavior of other agents based on anticipated trees, and by focusing on states critical for interactions. Our results show that both algorithms perform better than the baselines, and MAVIPER-trained agents achieve more coordinated performance than IVIPER-trained agents in multi-agent environments.

The explanation processes of neural language models are difficult to interpret, but recent progress has been made in automatically generating machine rationales of their behavior, particularly in relation to their in-distribution generalization.  However, less attention has been paid to utilizing these rationales to improve their performance, especially in out-of-distribution settings, and how explanation regularization can impact this improvement. We aim to fill this knowledge gap by introducing ER-TEST, an evaluation protocol designed to assess explanation regularization models' generalization capabilities outside of their training data across various dimensions and testing methods, and through ER-TEST, our study investigates the effects of various factors, including the effectiveness of different explanation regularization criteria, the number and choice of human-labeled rationales in the training data, and the use of distantly-supervised rationales, and the results show that while it has little impact on in-distribution performance, it can significantly improve performance in out-of-distribution settings, and the effectiveness of regularization can depend on the specific task at hand and the availability of high-quality training data.

A significant difficulty in reinforcement learning is defining tasks that can be both comprehensively understood and verifiably correct.  To overcome this obstacle, researchers often define tasks through a framework known as reward machines - a type of finite state machine that encapsulates the task to be accomplished.  To improve this process, a novel approach called skill machines is introduced, a type of representation that can be learned directly from reward machines that specify how a particular task should be solved.  By proposing a framework in which an agent first acquires a group of foundational skills within an environment without a reward system, and then combines these skills using a learned skill machine, the agent is able to create more intricate behaviors that correspond to a wide range of logical specifications, including complex, long-duration tasks.  By demonstrating the effectiveness of this strategy in both simple and high-dimensional environments like video games, the results suggest that the agent is able to create optimal behaviors for a wide variety of tasks, all in the absence of additional learning or data.  Finally, the study reveals that, by using common reinforcement learning algorithms in offline settings, the agent can significantly improve its performance when striving for optimal results.

This work focuses on the concentration phenomenon in discrete-time random systems with unbounded states. It introduces a novel functional analytical approach to derive exponential concentration inequalities, and also demonstrates that the existence of a certain type of Lyapunov function not only guarantees stability in these systems but also leads to exponential concentration inequalities when sampling from their stationary distributions, leveraging a transport-entropy inequality. These findings have significant implications for reinforcement learning and control, enabling exponential concentration inequalities for unbounded observables without assuming reversibility or precise knowledge of the random systems involved, departing from common concentration inequality assumptions in statistical mechanics and Markov diffusion processes.

Individuals acquainted with circuitry are familiar with the fundamental circuit components of capacitor, resistor, and inductor. However, Professor Leon Chua proposed the concept of a fourth fundamental element, known as the memristor, which is grounded in the theory of symmetry and relates flux to charge. Initially proposed in 1971, this theory gained practical validation in 2008 when researchers at HP Labs developed a physical model for the memristor. Characterized by variable resistance, flexibility, and no leakage current, memristors offer advantages that enable diverse applications such as memory, logic, and neuromorphic systems. By employing computer simulations using VerilogA models of memristors with sinusoidal inputs and various window functions, researchers can analyze circuit behavior to further develop the practical applications of these devices.

Federated learning's susceptibility to user privacy issues is compounded by the discovery that Vision Transformers are vulnerable to specific data inversion attacks. Our research demonstrates that the low-dimensional spatial priors embedded in the position encodings of Vision Transformers significantly accelerate training, but this comes at the cost of heightened position sensitivity, thereby compromising data privacy. To counter this risk, enhancing the position-insensitivity of Vision Transformer models has emerged as a compelling approach to safeguard data privacy against these gradient-based attacks. Nonetheless, simply eliminating the position encodings not only jeopardizes the convergence and accuracy of Vision Transformers but also exposes them to even greater privacy threats. To reconcile this dilemma, we introduce a novel Masked Jigsaw Puzzle (MJP) technique that severs the gradient-based privacy leakages inherent in Vision Transformers. MJP is seamlessly integratable into existing Vision Transformer variants and has been extensively tested to verify its efficacy in both boosting performance on large-scale datasets and significantly strengthening privacy preservation under typical gradient attacks. Our code is available on GitHub.

In most existing studies on Entity Linking, it is commonly assumed that a comprehensive reference database is readily available, ensuring that every mention can be successfully linked. However, in reality, databases often fall short and novel concepts emerge frequently, making this assumption unrealistic. To address this, this paper introduces the EDIN benchmark, where an existing entity linking system must integrate labeled mentions and unknown entities lacking descriptions in the database. By comparing EDIN with zero-shot entity linking, this paper highlights the distinct challenges EDIN presents. Based on a dense-retrieval based approach to entity linking, the EDIN pipeline is developed as a comprehensive system for identifying and cataloging unknown entities, organizing their mentions into meaningful groups, and linking relevant information. Experiment results reveal that creating a single unified embedding for each entity that consolidates information from multiple mentions yields more accurate outcomes than treating each mention as a separate entity.

Significant advancements in natural language processing tasks have been achieved through neural attention models. Nevertheless, the quadratic memory complexity of the self-attention module, particularly for lengthy inputs, poses a limitation in long text summarization applications. Instead of optimizing the attention module, we investigate whether restricted contextual models can perform comparably to those that maintain a comprehensive global context by viewing the input as a unified sequence. Our approach is centered around dividing the input into sections based on the principle of locality during both the encoding and decoding processes, treating each section as a separate page. We have experimented with different degrees of granularity, including sentences and documents, in text summarization to evaluate three kinds of locality. Our findings indicate that our locality-aware model outperforms strong baselines equipped with efficient attention modules, while our analysis provides deeper insights into our modeling strategy.

Recent advancements in Natural Language Processing have led to significant gains by Large Language Models in many benchmark tests. However, the escalating cost, time consumption, and environmental impact of constantly creating larger models have necessitated the search for an alternative solution. This research examines whether it's feasible to rephrase questions in accordance with the model's capabilities, thereby rendering them easier to solve. To this end, our study investigates whether it's possible to break down complex questions into simpler ones, thereby improving model performance. In a comprehensive analysis across a diverse array of datasets involving various reasoning patterns, our results demonstrate that this question decomposition approach yields notable enhancements of 24% for GPT3 and 29% for RoBERTa-SQuAD, even in conjunction with an in-built calculator. Furthermore, our approach facilitates human involvement in the research, suggesting that it could provide a practical alternative to developing larger Language Models, a notion supported by our concept of Human-in-the-loop Question Decomposition. The relevant code and data are available at https://github.com/Pruthvi98/QuestionDecomposition.

Surveys serve as vital evidence in policymaking, decision-making, and societal understanding, yet collecting large datasets for reliable subpopulation estimates proves costly and time-consuming. A novel approach called Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP) can provide accurate subpopulation estimates using reduced datasets. Research has extensively utilized graphical displays to convey and assess MRP estimates; however, there has been limited investigation into how visualization should be implemented in this context. This study conducts a systematic literature review to evaluate current MRP visualization practices. Furthermore, by applying MRP to the U.S. 2016 presidential election data, this research aims to demonstrate the consequences of current visualization approaches and explore potential enhancements. Our findings indicate that uncertainty is often overlooked, although it plays a crucial role in survey inference. A choropleth map is commonly used, yet it primarily displays point estimates and might obscure essential information. This study demonstrates that visualizing uncertainty can highlight the impact of model specifications on the estimation result, also suggesting a visualization strategy to account for the bias-variance trade-off in MRP model evaluation.

As technology shrinks, it creates issues such as radiation-caused faults in critical and hostile settings, like space. This affects system design. This study introduces an architectural approach to enhance fault-tolerance in processor clusters, where a six-core open-source RISC-V processor is upgraded with an innovative 'On-Demand Redundancy Grouping' technique called ODRG. The ODRG scheme enables a cluster to either run two resilient cores or six individual cores, achieving a balance between high-performance and limited operational overhead, with the ability to switch modes during runtime. The ODRG unit requires a small area - around 1% of the cluster total, adding less than 11% of a core's area per three-core grouping - and incurs negligible timing penalties, surpassing a commercial state-of-the-art model in terms of fault recovery. Furthermore, unlike other fault-tolerance solutions, ODRG's redundancy can be utilized for independent computations, leading to a notable 2.96 times boost in performance for certain applications.

Calculating the similarity between terms, text data, and concepts is a crucial task in various text-based applications, including knowledge acquisition, recommendation systems, and natural language processing. In recent years, many structured knowledge representations, known as ontologies, have been developed for information systems and used to represent knowledge bases. Building upon this foundation, researchers have advanced the calculation of semantic similarity derived from ontologies, which can be further enhanced by incorporating other similarity metrics depending on the application context. In this paper, we present an approach to calculating semantic similarity based on ontologies for a recommendation system context.

A new method for learning set generation is presented, which addresses the limitation of sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) models that fail to fully exploit the key properties of sets, particularly order-invariance and cardinality. The approach samples meaningful orders from the large space of possible set arrangements and models the size and content of the generated sets together, allowing any Seq2Seq model to benefit from the incorporation of these set properties through a model-independent data augmentation strategy. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that training with the proposed data augmentation method leads to an average relative improvement of 20% across a range of Seq2Seq models including BART, T5, and GPT-3. The method is available via the SETAUG tool at https://setgen.structgen.com.

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models have achieved notable success in generation tasks by modeling the reverse process of gradually diffusing data into a Gaussian distribution. To generate a sample in these models, the process of iteratively denoising Gaussian noise is performed. However, the practical application of this method involves a significant time commitment due to the hundreds to thousands of steps required, which results in extremely low efficiency during inference. To improve this efficiency, a novel acceleration strategy called Early-Stopped DDPM is proposed, which involves terminating the diffusion process after initial steps and beginning the reverse denoising process from a non-Gaussian distribution. When combined with pre-trained generative models, the sampling process from a target distribution can be efficiently completed by diffusing samples from these models, thereby substantially reducing the number of required denoising steps. Consequently, the sample quality of Early-Stopped DDPM is enhanced and outperforms the baseline methods, including both vanilla DDPM and the adopted pre-trained generative model. Through experiments on diverse datasets including CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet, Early-Stopped DDPM demonstrates its potential to accelerate model performance while also offering attractive features, including independence from existing acceleration techniques and the ability to control image generation at both the global and pixel level.

Recent successes of Deep Neural Networks in hyperspectral image classification have largely been based on general architectures, which neglect the inherent characteristics of these images, such as noise patterns. Consequently, prior models struggle to produce distinctive features, leading to disappointing classification outcomes. To effectively exploit this intrinsic information, a novel deep learning approach is introduced, which incorporates a noise-sensitive module and denoising framework specifically tailored for hyperspectral image classification. Initially, a noise-based model is developed to describe the spectral signatures of these images, capturing their inherent class variations and overlaps. A noise-sensitive module is then designed to isolate physical noise within each object, followed by a denoising framework to remove these disturbances. The proposed CNN framework is thus optimized to produce robust features, yielding improved classification performance. Empirical evaluations on two prominent datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach. The source code and implementations of this method and comparative models can be accessed at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/shendu-sw/noise-physical-framework.

In situations where data storage qubits are kept in isolated conditions, using minimal measurements and controls, effective noise reduction is achievable through additional probes that are applied only when necessary. For solid-state qubits, specifically, we examined dephasing noise generated by a two-state fluctuator, utilizing a theoretical noise reduction approach with a qubit-based probe, known as a spectator qubit. Assuming projective measurements of the SQ, our analysis involves deriving the performance of various strategies in scenarios where noise reduction works effectively. Initially, we explored the 'Greedy' strategy, which prioritizes maximizing the data qubit coherence at any given moment, and found it to be highly effective. Additionally, through analytical methods, including Bayesian maps, we designed a one-parameter family of algorithms that can approximate this 'Greedy' strategy. In situations with extremely high noise sensitivity, our one-parameter family reduces the data qubit decoherence rate in accordance with the square of its sensitivity, and we named the optimal algorithm as Map-based Optimized Adaptive Algorithm for Asymptotic Regime. It was also demonstrated that the MOAAAR outperforms the 'Greedy' strategy, particularly in scenarios with high noise sensitivity of the SQ, through both numerical and analytical methods.

A key message of the slogan "nobody is safe until everybody is safe" is that a unified global approach is necessary to address global issues like pandemics in a connected world, exemplified by COVID-19. Focusing on the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, our study investigates the spread of an infectious virus across interconnected communities. Considering populations with varying vaccination rates, ranging from unvaccinated ("Bronze"), moderately vaccinated ("Silver"), to well-vaccinated ("Gold") groups, and different network configurations for virus transmission, our analysis reveals a critical issue: when "Bronze" communities interact with "Silver" and "Gold" ones, they significantly contribute to increased infections in the latter. Notably, this phenomenon highlights the detrimental impact of unvaccinated communities on those that are vaccinated. When we analyze the spread of the virus across different network configurations, two factors play a crucial role: the strength of interactions and the network density. Specifically, in networks such as Barabasi-Albert, our study shows that "Gold" communities perform the best in controlling infection rates, while even a few unvaccinated ("Bronze") communities can trigger a surge in infections among moderately and well-vaccinated communities. Furthermore, when comparing various network configurations, including dense Erdos-Renyi, sparse Watts-Strogatz, and Barabasi-Albert networks, our study reveals that dense Erdos-Renyi networks can achieve a disease-free state, while the sparse Watts-Strogatz and Barabasi-Albert networks struggle to do so, unless all communities within the network become fully vaccinated.

We conducted a theoretical investigation on the $D\bar{D}K$ three-body system using a fixed-center approximation to the Faddeev equations, incorporating the interaction between $D$ and $K$, and $D$ and $\bar{D}$ from a chiral unitary approach. We analyzed the $K$ meson's scattering off a clusterized $D\bar{D}$ system, which may form a scalar meson $X(3720)$. Due to the strong $DK$ interaction, where a dynamically generated scalar $D^*_{s0}(2317)$ meson appears, a resonance pattern emerges in the $K$-$(D\bar{D})_{X(3720)}$ scattering amplitude. This result corroborates the possibility of a $D\bar{D}K$ bound state and aligns with prior theoretical findings suggesting the existence of a new hidden charm $K$ meson, specifically $K_{c\bar{c}}(4180)$ with quantum numbers $I(J^P) = \frac{1}{2}(0^-)$ and a mass of about $4180$ MeV. Consequently, it is hoped that these theoretical predictions will drive efforts to detect it experimentally.

In a sequential dynamic resource allocation problem with T divisible resources and n fixed agents, the resources are assigned according to agents' stochastic utilities drawn from a known distribution, with immediate and irreversible decisions made. This study differs from other works which prioritize overall efficiency over fairness by aiming for egalitarian welfare instead. We begin with a fluid-based approach derived from the problem's deterministic approximation and show it can achieve an allocation that incurs regret of approximately $O(\sqrt{T})$ compared to the optimal outcome. To achieve lower regret, we then propose a new policy called $\mathsf{BIRT}$ which refines its allocation solution at most $O(\log\log T)$ times. We prove that the $\mathsf{BIRT}$ policy can obtain $O(1)$ regret in relation to the hindsight optimum regardless of time horizon $T$ length and starting point, and also validate this through simulations comparing it to various benchmarks policies and observe substantial improvements.

As autonomous systems continue to advance, safety issues emerge when operating in unpredictable environments. This research aims to mitigate these concerns by introducing a safety feature for mechanical systems that identifies and addresses instability caused by external disruptions. This safety feature can be integrated independently with existing nominal control systems and limits power transfer if the system's reaction would result in instability. This method utilizes the computation of the Largest Lyapunov Exponent (LLE), a measure of dynamic divergence or convergence rates, to rapidly detect divergent system behaviors. By integrating the LLE with Control Barrier Functions, power limitations can be imposed on systems controlled by jerks. The proposed safety architecture has been tested on an Omnidirectional Micro Aerial Vehicle (OMAV) under both free flight and interactive conditions.

We are looking at a classic problem of dividing a divisible and heterogeneous resource among a number of individuals, using the analogy of a cake that can be divided into pieces.  In our version of the problem, individuals are not isolated but are embedded on a graph, meaning that each individual only compares their portion of the cake to the portions of their neighbors.  Our main goal is to find a fair way of dividing the cake among the individuals on the graph so that each individual is happy with their portion and doesn't envy the portions of their neighbors.

We also look at how much computational work (or number of queries) is required to find a fair way of dividing the cake among the individuals on the graph.  In our main contribution, we identify a simple graph structure where this problem can be solved very efficiently, using no more than O(n^3 * log(n)) computational work.  In certain cases of this graph structure, even less computational work (specifically, O(n^2)) may be needed to find a fair way of dividing the cake among the individuals on the graph.  On the other hand, if the graph is a very specific type of tree, then we can prove that at least a certain minimum amount (specifically, Ω(n^2)) of computational work is required to find a fair way of dividing the cake among the individuals on the graph.

Current approaches to cybersecurity threat and risk analysis automate only parts of the process, forcing teams to rely on expert judgment for key decisions during the software development cycle. In reality, teams of experts engage in face-to-face analysis sessions to determine system design, which is often subjective and prone to biases due to underrepresented diversity within security teams. The influence of non-technical threat perceptions on risk analysis has been researched, but no studies have examined the effect of diversity on analyzing technical security artefacts. To fill this knowledge gap, this study aims to establish a methodology to identify the critical factors contributing to diversity in risk analysis.

This paper tackles the issue of reduced performance in 5G networks due to user mobility in complex multi-antenna systems. It introduces a cutting-edge method, called Multi-Dimensional Matrix Pencil (MDMP), to predict channels by utilizing frequency-angle and time-angle relationships of wideband signals. MDMP also incorporates a new approach to pairing time delays and Doppler effects through angle estimation. By accounting for realistic user movements affecting path delays, our approach outperforms existing methods in time-varying scenarios. It is theoretically proven that our prediction method achieves zero error when the number of base station antennas increases, requiring only a couple of initial channel samples. Moreover, a performance bound for the minimum number of base station antennas needed for satisfactory performance is established. Simulation results using industrial 3GPP channel models show that our proposed MDMP method achieves almost the same level of performance as a stationary scenario even at 120 km/h and with a latency of 16 ms.

Personalizing interactions between humans and virtual agents involves several key factors, one of which is modeling the behavior style of virtual agents. To effectively achieve this, our proposed machine learning approach synthesizes gestures by leveraging prosodic features and text styles from diverse speakers. The model's architecture, built using data from the PATS database, enables zero-shot multimodal style transfer and successfully generalizes to unseen speakers. We view style as an integral part of communicative behavior, coloring the expressivity of speech content while text and multimodal signals convey the message. By decoupling content from style, our system can infer style embeddings for unseen speakers without the need for retraining. The model's primary objectives are: first, generating the gestures of a source speaker based on their audio and text input; second, conditioning the source speaker's gestures on the style embedding of a target speaker; and third, enabling zero-shot style transfer for speakers unseen during training. Our system comprises two key components: a style encoder network that generates a fixed dimensional style embedding from a target speaker's multimodal data and a sequence-to-sequence synthesis network that synthesizes gestures conditioned on the style embedding. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through its ability to synthesize gestures of a source speaker and transfer knowledge of target speaker style variability in a zero-shot setting, producing 3D animations of 2D gestures and conduct evaluations to validate our approach and compare it to a baseline model.

Consider a non-trivial subgroup H of a finite group G with identity element e. We define a specific type of graph, the generalized non-coprime graph GAmma, with vertices as the non-identity elements of G. In this graph, two elements are connected by an edge if they share a common divisor greater than one and one of them belongs to subgroup H. This paper explores properties of these graphs, focusing on their structure in cyclic groups, where we determine conditions for GAmma to be one of several predefined graph types. We also examine how properties change when considering a broader class of finite groups, specifically nilpotent groups, and present contrasting behavior for groups with elements of prime power order, before concluding with a connection to another related graph, the Gruenberg--Kegel graph.

A compartmental model for COVID-19 based on nonlinear partial differential equations continuously tracks the spread of the virus in space and over time. Enhancing the model with detailed subcategories, increasing the resolution of geographical locations, and adding more compartments significantly increases the number of unknown variables to millions. A high-performance parallel solver was developed to quickly process large models of high accuracy. The solver combines advanced techniques, such as domain decomposition and multigrid methods, to ensure scalability and efficient results. A specific numerical example uses a five-stage COVID-19 model for Southern Ontario to showcase the proposed solver's capability and performance in large geographical areas. The results demonstrate the potential for predicting COVID-19 infections three months in advance with a system size of 92 million people within just 7 hours using 1780 processes, greatly reducing the time-consuming computations required by traditional solvers.

Dorigoni, Green, and Wen have proposed an exact integrated correlator formula for four superconformal operators in the $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Our work focuses on the large N limit of their formula, revealing it to be equivalent to a sum of contributions from $(p,q)$-strings due to SL(2,Z) duality. This allows us to express all terms using a single function akin to the fundamental string contribution. Analyzing its perturbative expansion, we uncovered the large N non-perturbative corrections and interpret them as D3-brane instantons in the holographic type IIB string theory. Additionally, solving the Laplace-difference equation for the correlator confirms these findings.

Investigating the development of pre-stellar clouds demands advanced observational capabilities, particularly in high-mass star-forming regions. Our goal is to assess how precisely physical properties of massive star-forming clouds can be deduced from observations, focusing on the capabilities of the Next Generation VLA interferometer. Utilizing magnetohydrodynamic simulation data and a filamentary cloud structure mimicking an infrared-dark cloud, we simulate synthetic ngVLA observations of spectral lines and examine the resulting column density, gas temperature, and kinematics. Our findings are compared against both ideal observations and the actual three-dimensional model. The ngVLA's high resolution of 0.01 pc allows for the mapping of cloud kinematics and structure at sub-arcsecond scales, even for complex molecules like HCO+, NH3, and N2H+, down to 4 kpc. NH3 maps and temperature measurements are achieved with 1 K precision across a 15 x 40 arcsecond area, while higher frequencies suffer from large-scale emission loss. Line observations closely replicate cloud kinematics, except on the largest scales, where line-of-sight confusion introduces interpretive complications. The ngVLA will provide precise data on cloud structure and chemical states in high-mass star-forming regions, albeit complemented by single-dish data to estimate large-scale properties and total column densities.

To achieve highly reliable low-latency communication systems with high efficiency and robust security, a comprehensive approach to optimizing downlink transmissions is developed, especially in situations with multiple users and potential eavesdroppers. This optimization problem involves maximizing a collective secrecy transmission rate while minimizing both the maximum transmission error rate and potential security breaches, achieved through a novel precoder design. Due to its complexities and non-linear nature, the multi-objective problem is addressed by applying a two-phase optimization process, starting with a precoder optimization and followed by a transmission error rate minimization and security leak reduction phase. This process allows for a deeper analysis of local optima through a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker condition and a generalized eigenvalue solution, further validated through a series of simulations.

To quantify the entanglement between static black holes, we compare two maximally-extended spacetime regions divided by the event horizon. Starting with the Schwarzschild black hole, our investigation extends to other cases, including charged black holes with more than one horizon, and we also examine the scenario under F(R) gravity with spherical symmetry. Using the replica trick, we calculate the entanglement entropy based on the specific replica spacetime for each black hole type, and we find that it conforms to the Bekenstein-Hawking area law for spherically-symmetric and static black holes.

Deep learning models have achieved impressive results across diverse tasks, but their robustness has been undermined by adversarial attacks. These sophisticated assaults subtly alter an input image, rendering it almost imperceptible to the human eye, yet drastically altering the network's classification outcome. This study investigates the Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attack and the Adaptive Mask Segmentation Attack (ASMA) against the image segmentation model DeepLabV3, employing MobileNetV3 and ResNet50 architectures, and found that PGD consistently achieves the desired segmentation outcome, whereas ASMA's effectiveness in targeting multiple classes was less reliable. Nonetheless, the vulnerability inherent to such attacks jeopardizes the security of image classification deep learning models in general.

This research introduces a highly scalable and efficient approach to real-time
bidding, where the exploration strategy is guided by the predictive confidence of
models predicting click-through rates and operates effectively within high-throughput
and low-latency settings. Our findings, confirmed through rigorous online A/B
testing, show that incorporating uncertainty-driven exploration leads to improved
model performance and enhanced business metrics.

A significant hurdle in computational biology is to reconcile the need for high-quality, high-quantity data with models that accurately capture biological complexities. Although tools such as identifiability analysis and information criteria help bridge this gap, limitations persist when trying to reconcile the amount of available data with the level of detail needed to answer pressing biological questions. Simple, phenomenological models often provide the only viable options, such as the logistic and Gompertz growth models, which can be identified from typical experimental measurements. However, to derive insights from complex, non-identifiable models that incorporate key biological mechanisms, we study the geometric relationship between these complex models and simpler, identifiable surrogates. By exploring the quantitative links between non-identifiable and identifiable parameters, we establish a middle ground that bridges the non-identifiable parameters and conventional identifiability metrics. Our approach is illustrated through a series of mathematical models examining multicellular tumour spheroid growth. Characterized by limited, noisy data, tumour spheroid experiments necessitate the development of overly complex models, making our geometric method particularly useful in predicting non-identifiabilities, partitioning non-identifiable parameter spaces into identifiable subsets, and extracting additional biological insights from complex, non-identifiable models.

Calculations for the nucleosynthesis of heavy elements depend heavily on the photon strength functions, whose relation to photoabsorption cross sections allows researchers to experimentally validate them. A study investigated the photoresponse of $^{66}$Zn within the 5.6 MeV to 9.9 MeV energy range and analyzed the "elastic" decay channel that leads back to the nucleus's ground state, separating electric and magnetic dipole transitions in the process. Using a high-intensity, linearly-polarized quasi-monoenergetic photon beam, nuclear resonance fluorescence experiments were conducted on $^{66}$Zn and the extracted data used to calculate the photoabsorption cross section and the branching ratio back to the ground state. Compared to a previous experiment involving bremsstrahlung, the new findings indicate significantly lower cross sections, suggesting that estimates from statistical-model calculations underestimated the branching ratio in the previous analysis.

Object localization using coarse annotations such as categories is an arduous task that requires precise object identification. Current deep network approaches primarily employ class activation maps that pinpoint object discriminative areas, but neglect to encompass the entire object. The recent rise of transformer-based techniques has led to an increased emphasis on background, thus hindering complete object identification. To address these limitations, a re-attention mechanism called token refinement transformer (TRT) is proposed to harness object-level semantics and improve localization performance. The TRT model incorporates a new module called token priority scoring module (TPSM) to suppress background noise and focus on target objects. Furthermore, a class activation map is integrated to semantically inform attention and restrain it to the target object. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets confirm the superiority of the proposed TRT approach over existing image categorization-based methods. The accompanying source code can be accessed through the link provided at https://github.com/su-hui-zz/ReAttentionTransformer.

Recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown impressive results across multiple domains, yet they remain susceptible to noisy and adversarial data. Developing effective GNN defenses against such threats is crucial, but existing solutions are resource-intensive and not easily scalable. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for strengthening GNN resilience, referred to as the Weighted Laplacian GNN (RWL-GNN). The proposed method leverages the beneficial properties of the Laplacian matrix to formulate an optimized framework that effectively discards adversarial/noisy connections and adjusts graph weights. We successfully demonstrate the efficacy of RWL-GNN using the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN) architecture, but its adaptability allows it to integrate with any existing GNN architecture. Simulation results on benchmark datasets validate the proposed method's performance in both accuracy and computational efficiency, with accompanying code available at https://github.com/Bharat-Runwal/RWL-GNN.

Ensuring the accurate tracking of competitor vehicles surrounding an autonomous car is essential for successful and efficient decision-making in high-speed racing. Deep neural networks, although powerful, pose challenges due to their black-box nature in high-stakes applications like autonomous driving. To address this limitation, our approach develops a structured framework for forecasting opposing car trajectories using deep neural networks, ensuring that predicted paths are constrained. This constraint allows for reliable performance guarantees. We tested our method against a comparable model, an LSTM-based encoder-decoder architecture, utilizing data from detailed Hardware-in-the-Loop simulations. The results show that our approach provides better prediction accuracy while maintaining the required performance guarantees. This achievement validates the practicality of deploying our model in real-world autonomous racing. Furthermore, our developed model was successfully implemented on a car by the Technical University of Munich for the Indy Autonomous Challenge 2021. The research code can be accessed as open-source at www.github.com/TUMFTM/MixNet.

Research on galaxy structure often suggests a division between star-forming and passive galaxies, with disks and spheroids respectively characterizing their shapes. However, a comprehensive study using MaNGA data reveals a more complex galaxy population. By analyzing the kinematic properties of 4,574 local galaxies, it was discovered that galaxies at a fixed mass range exhibit a continuous and not bimodal distribution in rotation velocity versus dispersion ratio. Furthermore, it was observed that fast-rotating galaxies can be grouped into two categories, with dynamically-cold disks making up the majority. This study also showed that, while disks make up most star-forming galaxies, passive galaxies have a more varied composition, with around 30% comprising passive disks, a proportion significantly higher than slow rotators. These findings indicate that a significant portion of galaxies in the local universe are disks, with most transforming into less rotation-supported systems following the suppression of star formation, while spheroids remain a minority and not the typical outcome for galaxy evolution.

Tractable density models called normalizing flows can approximate intricate distributions, such as those of complex physical systems. Nevertheless, the existing methods for training flows either lead to the problem of mode-seeking, rely on samples generated by costly simulations, or make use of loss functions with significant variability. In an attempt to circumvent these issues, flows are now combined with annealed importance sampling (AIS), which reduces the variance of the importance weight by minimizing the mass-covering $\alpha$-divergence when $\alpha=2$. This new approach, termed Flow AIS Bootstrap (FAB), leverages AIS to generate samples in areas where the flow underperforms in approximating the target, thereby enabling the detection of new modes. The proposed method has been applied to the approximation of complex multimodal targets, yielding highly accurate results that surpass previous techniques. Furthermore, FAB has achieved the milestone of learning the Boltzmann distribution of the alanine dipeptide molecule using solely the unnormalized target density, without recourse to simulations. By outperforming maximum likelihood training on samples generated by molecular dynamics simulations and utilizing significantly fewer evaluations, FAB has produced remarkably accurate results. Ultimately, the implementation of FAB has yielded unbiased histograms of dihedral angles for the alanine dipeptide molecule, displaying almost perfect correspondence with ground truth after the samples have been reweighted using importance weights.

Capturing users' diverse behaviors is a crucial component of modern e-commerce, mainly applied in optimizing the joint predictions of click-through and conversion rates. Many current approaches disregard the significant impacts of two critical user behavior characteristics: for a given item list, users' actions are influenced not only by the item itself, but also by their past interactions on other items within the sequence; (i) users' behaviors occur across various time scales, such as frequent clicking versus infrequent purchasing. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel user behavior network named HEROES, incorporating contextual information to analyze users' behaviors at multiple scales. By establishing a hierarchical framework with lower and upper layers modeling engagement and satisfaction behaviors respectively, the model can learn suitable time scales for each layer, automatically adapting to the dynamic nature of user behaviors. Furthermore, the model includes a novel recurrent unit based on the Hawkes process that encodes both items' context and users' past interactions. By integrating the model with survival analysis, it can be applied in unbiased ranking systems. Experiments conducted on three large-scale datasets demonstrate HEROES' superiority compared to the current state-of-the-art methods.

The Lightning Network (LN) has rapidly expanded and is now the preferred scaling solution for the Bitcoin blockchain. LN's reliability relies on its nodes being able to settle balances by confirming Bitcoin blockchain transactions within a predetermined timeframe. A built-in time constraint inherent to the LN makes it susceptible to malicious attacks that aim to overload the Bitcoin blockchain and disrupt its operations. We examine LN's vulnerability to "mass exit" attacks conducted by a small group of malicious nodes that compel a large number of honest users to interact with the blockchain. Specifically, we analyze two types of attacks: first, a "zombie" attack where a set of nodes deliberately shut down to hold funds in channels for longer than allowed; second, a "mass double-spend" attack where a set of nodes submit multiple transactions for channels with expired states, prompting a surge in incorrect submissions from honest users. Using simulations, we demonstrate that these attacks can be carried out effectively by a relatively small group under conditions of high congestion and mild statistical assumptions about channel balances. We achieved these findings by modeling the problem as a graph cut problem for identifying a worst-case group of malicious nodes. These results are supported by theoretical justification based on the LN's scale-free network topology.

A photometric search has been conducted to identify cataclysmic variable stars, focusing specifically on potential AR Scorpii-type binaries. We analyzed data from GAIA and identified promising candidates that correspond to unidentified X-ray sources, and subsequently inspected their light curves taken by various observatories. From our research, eight sources emerged as CV candidates, with six new discoveries and two previously recognized as CVs but requiring further study. We found two systems exhibiting eclipses and tied to unidentified XMM-Newton or Swift sources, and also identified a candidate for a polar linked with an unknown ASKA source. Two polar candidates are potentially located within the so-called period gap of CV systems, and six others display orbital periods below this gap. Although we didn't find a suitable candidate for AR Scorpii-type binaries, our research indicates that surveys may have overlooked CV systems emitting X-rays but lacking frequent outbursts.

Most theoretical studies of shear instability in layered fluids assume that shear stress and buoyancy forces act at the same interface. However, in this discussion, we investigate how discrepancies between these interfaces impact shear instability. Employing both linear mathematical analysis and advanced computer simulations, we found that shear instability with unequal forces combines properties from both the Holmboe and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities, and developed a method to identify whether the instability behaves more similarly to either of these phenomena. Furthermore, the presence of asymmetry leads to mixing patterns characterized by both upwelling and erosion-like flows, and it often realigns the shear stress and buoyancy forces. Notably, in almost all but perfectly symmetrical Kelvin-Helmholtz simulations, the distribution of the Richardson number tends to collapse, indicating that asymmetry reduces the influence of specific characteristics of shear stress and stratification on turbulent mixing events. The dependence of the observed turbulent behavior on small-scale details of shear stress and stratification has important implications for analyzing oceanographic data.

Recent advances in unpaired image denoising show considerable potential.
However, the effectiveness of most methods hinges on uncertain assumptions about noise patterns.
A structural approach rather than focusing on noise statistics may lead to a more dependable solution.
In light of this, we present a self-supervised, unpaired denoising technique based on a degradation and refinement framework. 
This novel method outperforms existing techniques and demonstrates consistent performance across various datasets.

A transmembrane integrin protein plays a vital role in cell structure, influencing the cell's interaction with its surrounding matrix by altering its cytoskeleton and cell membrane adhesion through complex biochemical mechanisms. In areas where integrin activity is prominent, the formation of specific lipid groups, which are crucial for certain endocytosis processes, occurs. To gain a deeper understanding of these dynamics, researchers developed a model to study the interaction between integrin activity states and the membrane's natural movements. This model provides a detailed, mathematically precise explanation of how integrin affects the membrane's shape, movement, and clustering of lipids, highlighting the complex relationship between these factors and various biological timescales.

On certain compact, orientable three-dimensional manifolds with intricate geometries, numerical solutions to Einstein's constraint equations are obtained, encompassing a straightforward constant mean curvature case and a more complex scenario where mean curvature varies. These constant mean curvature solutions derived on selected manifolds also fulfill the requirements of the Yamabe problem, which aims to transform an arbitrary geometry into one characterized by constant scalar curvature.

The concept of homophily suggests that similarity leads to connections. Mathematically, a network is considered homophilic if the clusters formed within it are denser than would be expected in a random distribution of the same cluster sizes. This idea is linked to a random coloring model for network homophily, which treats the vector of cluster sizes as the outcome of random cluster assignments. As a result, a network is deemed homophilic at a given significance level when the probability of observing the actual cluster size vector or one more extreme is lower than the chosen threshold. However, calculating this probability is an NP-hard problem, so we turn to a multidimensional version of Cantelli's inequality to find an upper bound. This bound, known as the homophily index, requires knowledge of the covariance matrix of the random vector. We fill this gap by determining this matrix within the random coloring model, which surprisingly only depends on the input partition and network degrees. This structure is then plugged into Cantelli's bound, producing a simple and meaningful measure of network homophily.

A generalized model of two-dimensional dilaton gravity, known as the Fabbri-Russo model, has parameters denoting different types of gravity, specifically the Russo-Susskind-Thorlacius model fitting one of them. The model examines the relationship between Page curves, entanglement islands, and black hole evaporation in eternal and evaporating black holes. The emergence of islands leads to decelerated entanglement entropy, supporting the principle of unitarity, with fine-grained entropy displaying unique behavior for each type of black hole. The parameter significantly influences the early Page curve, yet at late times, its effect becomes minimal. The relationship between entanglement islands and firewalls is also discussed, with the former being considered a more plausible explanation for entanglement-monogamy, followed by an analysis of the gravity/ensemble duality as a potential solution to the state conundrum caused by the island formula.

Event sequence modeling is typically carried out by using Temporal Point Process (TPP), which involves generating timestamps based on probabilistic models conditioned on historical influences.
While existing models often excel in fitting historical data, they fall short in generating timestamps that accurately mirror real-world events, thus necessitating improvement in predictive performance.
Inspired by deep generative models' success in image generation tasks, this work seeks to bridge the knowledge gap by developing a comprehensive and unified generative framework, termed Neural Temporal Point Process (GNTPP), to explore its feasibility and effectiveness in TPP event occurrence modeling.
To this end, the work introduces an innovative adaptive reweighting mechanism within attentive models to accurately account for the type and temporal relationships of historical events, thus providing a more accurate historical influence measurement.
The proposed framework is extensively evaluated using various generative probabilistic decoders and attention variants to demonstrate the significant improvements in predictive capabilities of the GNTPP model.
To our knowledge, this work presents the first-ever unified generative framework tailored to adapt to TPP event occurrence modeling and explores its efficacy in the field.
The codebase supporting the methods outlined in the work is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/BIRD-TAO/GNTPP} to facilitate future advancements in Neural TPPs.

In vehicular networks, Federated edge learning technology is viewed as a key to optimizing computation efficiency and safeguarding user privacy. The system enables vehicles to transmit data to edge servers, which process this data to update vehicle models, then sends the results back without compromising the original information. Despite this, the limited cache capacity and dynamic wireless channels in vehicular networks pose significant challenges when deciding the optimal number of participating vehicles. To further complicate matters, vehicles with diverse resource capacities influence training efficiency and accuracy, which in turn impact overall model precision. To address this, a novel vehicle selection algorithm is proposed that balances accuracy gains with cache stability, taking into consideration resource states of all nearby vehicles. The algorithm's performance is compared against existing standards through simulated experiments, showing it achieves superior results.
